name: ATMEGA32U4-MU
title: ATmega16U4/ATmega32U4 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 16/32 Kbytes Flash and full-speed USB device, 2.7 V to 5.5 V
summary: 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers with an on-chip USB 2.0 full-speed and low-speed device controller, running at up to 16 MHz (16 MIPS) from 2.7 V to 5.5 V. They carry 16 or 32 Kbytes of self-programmable Flash with a boot section and read-while-write, 1.25 or 2.5 Kbytes of SRAM, 512 bytes or 1 Kbyte of EEPROM, an 832-byte USB endpoint DPRAM, a PLL of 32 to 96 MHz for USB and a 10-bit high-speed timer, two 16-bit and one 8-bit timer, a USART with flow control, SPI, a two-wire interface, a 12-channel 10-bit ADC with differential gain stages, a temperature sensor, an analog comparator and JTAG with on-chip debug, on 26 I/O lines in 44-lead TQFP and QFN packages. ATMEGA32U4-MU is the 32 Kbyte part in the 7 x 7 mm 44-lead QFN for -40 °C to 85 °C, set up for an external crystal.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator connections
circuits.description: A quartz crystal or ceramic resonator between XTAL1 and XTAL2, each pin with a load capacitor to ground. C1 and C2 are kept equal; for crystals from 0.9 MHz to 16 MHz they start at 12 pF to 22 pF, the best value set by the crystal, stray capacitance and the noise around the board, while a ceramic resonator takes the values its own maker gives. A 32.768 kHz watch crystal on the low frequency oscillator is wired the same way.
notes: The low power crystal oscillator swings XTAL2 at reduced amplitude and cannot drive other clock inputs.

circuits.title: External clock drive configuration
circuits.description: An outside clock signal drives XTAL1 against the part's ground and XTAL2 is left open. The CKSEL fuses are set to 0000 to select this source. A step of more than 2% in frequency between one clock cycle and the next can upset the part, so larger changes are made with the part held in reset, or through the system clock prescaler.

circuits.title: Bus powered USB device with 5 V I/O
circuits.description: The part runs entirely from the USB cable: VBUS feeds UVCC, AVCC and VCC directly, so the I/O swing at about 5 V and the internal regulator makes the 3.0 V to 3.6 V USB pad supply, decoupled by the 1 µF capacitor on UCAP. Each data line has a 22 Ω series resistor between connector and pin. A crystal with two load capacitors gives the clock needed for full speed.
notes: The ATmega16U4/32U4 has no UID pin, so the connector's ID contact goes nowhere on the part.
A 10 µF capacitor on VBUS is strongly recommended; D+ and D- run short and as a matched differential pair from the connector, and transient or ESD suppressors may be added on the USB lines.

circuits.title: Bus powered USB device with 3 V I/O
circuits.description: Powered from the USB cable with the logic at 3 V: VBUS feeds UVCC, so the internal regulator still makes the USB pad supply on UCAP, while an outside 3 V regulator fed from VBUS supplies AVCC and VCC. 22 Ω resistors sit in series with D+ and D-, and a crystal with load capacitors clocks the part.
notes: The ATmega16U4/32U4 has no UID pin, so the connector's ID contact goes nowhere on the part.
A 10 µF capacitor on VBUS is strongly recommended; D+ and D- run short and as a matched differential pair from the connector, and transient or ESD suppressors may be added on the USB lines.

circuits.title: Self powered USB device with 3.4 V to 5.5 V I/O
circuits.description: The part takes its power from its own 3.4 V to 5.5 V supply on UVCC, AVCC and VCC, and VBUS is used only to sense the cable. The internal regulator makes the USB pad supply on UCAP from UVCC. 22 Ω resistors sit in series with D+ and D-, and a crystal with load capacitors clocks the part.
notes: The ATmega16U4/32U4 has no UID pin, so the connector's ID contact goes nowhere on the part.
A 10 µF capacitor on VBUS is strongly recommended; D+ and D- run short and as a matched differential pair from the connector, and transient or ESD suppressors may be added on the USB lines.

circuits.title: Self powered USB device with 3.0 V to 3.6 V I/O
circuits.description: With its own 3.0 V to 3.6 V supply the part runs USB without the internal regulator: UVCC is left open and the supply goes straight to UCAP, AVCC and VCC, with the 1 µF capacitor on UCAP. VBUS only senses the cable. 22 Ω resistors sit in series with D+ and D-, and a crystal with load capacitors clocks the part.
notes: The ATmega16U4/32U4 has no UID pin, so the connector's ID contact goes nowhere on the part.
A 10 µF capacitor on VBUS is strongly recommended; D+ and D- run short and as a matched differential pair from the connector, and transient or ESD suppressors may be added on the USB lines.

circuits.title: ADC power connections
circuits.description: AVCC is fed from the digital VCC through a 10 µH inductor and decoupled by 100 nF to the analog ground plane, an LC filter that keeps digital noise off the ADC supply. The GND pin beside AVCC returns to the same analog ground.
notes: VCC is pin 34, AVCC pin 44 and GND pin 43.
AVCC on the ADC8 to ADC13 side (pin 24) takes the same filter.

operation.text: AVR RISC core with 135 instructions, most of them one clock long, 32 general 8-bit working registers, fully static operation and an on-chip multiplier taking two cycles; throughput reaches 16 MIPS at 16 MHz. Flash endurance is 10,000 write/erase cycles and EEPROM 100,000. A boot section with its own lock bits allows in-system programming by an on-chip boot program with true read-while-write, and a programming lock protects the code. Parts clocked from an external crystal come with a USB boot loader already programmed. JTAG (IEEE 1149.1) gives boundary scan, on-chip debug, and a way to program the Flash, EEPROM, fuses and lock bits.

USB 2.0 full-speed and low-speed device module, with an interrupt when a transfer completes, at 12 Mbit/s or 1.5 Mbit/s. Endpoint 0 handles control transfers of up to 64 bytes; six more endpoints are programmable as IN or OUT for bulk, interrupt or isochronous transfers, each up to 256 bytes in double-bank mode, sharing an independent 832-byte DPRAM. It has suspend and resume interrupts, can reset the CPU when a bus reset is detected, connects or disconnects from the bus at the firmware's request, takes its 48 MHz full-speed clock from the PLL, and can run low speed without a crystal.

On-chip PLL from 32 to 96 MHz for USB and the high-speed timer. One 8-bit timer/counter with its own prescaler and compare mode; two 16-bit timer/counters with prescaler, compare and capture; one 10-bit high-speed timer/counter clocked from the PLL (64 MHz) with compare. PWM: four 8-bit channels, four with resolution programmable from 2 to 16 bits, and six high-speed channels programmable from 2 to 11 bits. Also an output compare modulator, a 12-channel 10-bit ADC with differential channels and programmable gain, a USART with hardware flow control, a master/slave SPI, a byte-oriented two-wire interface, a watchdog with its own oscillator, an analog comparator, pin-change interrupts that also wake the part, and a temperature sensor.

Power-on reset, a brown-out detector with programmable level, an internal calibrated 8 MHz oscillator, a clock prescaler with on-the-fly switching between the internal RC and an external oscillator, external and internal interrupt sources, and six sleep modes (Idle, Power-down, Power-save, ADC Noise Reduction, Standby, Extended Standby). Every I/O pairs a CMOS output with an LVTTL input.
Supply 2.7 V to 5.5 V over the industrial range, -40 °C to +85 °C. The maximum clock is 8 MHz at 2.7 V and 16 MHz at 4.5 V.

A low-power CMOS 8-bit microcontroller on the AVR enhanced RISC architecture. Most instructions take one clock, giving close to 1 MIPS per MHz, so speed can be traded against power. All 32 registers connect straight to the ALU, so one instruction reads two independent registers and finishes in a single cycle. Idle stops the CPU and keeps SRAM, timers, SPI and interrupts running; Power-down keeps register contents, stops the oscillator and waits for an interrupt or hardware reset; ADC Noise Reduction stops the CPU and every I/O module except the ADC; Standby keeps the crystal or resonator oscillator running while the rest sleeps, for a fast start. The Flash can be reprogrammed in system over SPI, by a conventional programmer, or by a boot program running on the core over any interface; code in the boot section keeps running while the application section is rewritten.

Ports B, C, D, E and F are bidirectional with a pull-up per bit, symmetrical drive with strong sink and source, and they go tri-state when reset becomes active even without a clock. An input with its pull-up on sources current when pulled low from outside. Port B drives harder than the other ports. Only PC6 and PC7 of port C, PE2 and PE6 of port E, and PF0, PF1 and PF4 to PF7 of port F reach the pins. Port F doubles as the ADC inputs and as the JTAG port; with JTAG enabled, the pull-ups on PF7 (TDI), PF5 (TMS) and PF4 (TCK) are on even through a reset.
Projected from reliability qualification: the retention failure rate stays well under 1 PPM for 20 years at 85 °C, and for 100 years at 25 °C.

Harvard design: program and data each have their own memory and bus. A single-level pipeline fetches the next instruction while the current one executes, so an instruction can finish on every clock. The register file holds 32 x 8-bit registers with single-cycle access: an ALU operation reads two operands, executes and writes the result back within one clock. R26 to R31 form the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers for indirect data addressing; Z also points into Flash for lookup tables. Jumps and calls reach the whole address space; most instructions are one 16-bit word, some are 32 bits. The SPM instruction that writes the application Flash section must sit in the boot section. Data space 0x20 - 0x5F holds the 64 I/O addresses; extended I/O at 0x60 - 0xFF in SRAM is reached only with ST/STS/STD and LD/LDS/LDD.

The ALU does arithmetic, logic and bit operations between two registers or a register and an immediate in one clock, plus single-register operations; the multiplier handles signed, unsigned and fractional formats. SREG reports the last arithmetic result after every ALU operation, which often saves a compare instruction. SREG is neither saved on interrupt entry nor restored on return: software does it. Its bits are I (global interrupt enable), T (bit copy storage for BLD/BST), H (half carry), S (N exclusive-or V), V (two's complement overflow), N (negative), Z (zero) and C (carry); all reset to 0. I is cleared by hardware when an interrupt is taken and set again by RETI; SEI and CLI set and clear it.

The register file supports one 8-bit operand with an 8-bit result, two 8-bit operands with an 8-bit result, two 8-bit operands with a 16-bit result, and one 16-bit operand with a 16-bit result. The 32 registers also occupy the first 32 data addresses (0x00 - 0x1F) without being SRAM, so X, Y and Z can index any register. The pointers support fixed displacement, post-increment and pre-decrement.

The stack lives in data SRAM and grows downward. The program must place it above 0x0100 before any call or enabled interrupt; SP starts at the last SRAM address. PUSH lowers SP by one and a call or interrupt by three; POP raises it by one and RET or RETI by three. SP is the pair SPH:SPL in I/O space. RAMPZ extends Z to 24 bits for ELPM and SPM (RAMPZ:ZH:ZL); LPM ignores it, and unused RAMPZ bits read zero and should be written zero.
The CPU runs on clkCPU, taken straight from the selected clock source with no internal division. Fetching the next instruction during execution of the current one gives up to 1 MIPS per MHz.

Each interrupt and the reset have their own vector at the bottom of program memory, and the lower the vector the higher the priority: RESET first, then INT0. Every interrupt has an enable bit that works together with I in SREG; with the boot lock bits BLB02 or BLB12 programmed, interrupts can be blocked depending on where the program counter is. IVSEL in MCUCR moves the vectors to the start of the boot section; the BOOTRST fuse moves the reset vector there. Taking an interrupt clears I; software may set it again to allow nesting, and RETI sets it. Flag-type interrupts set a flag that hardware clears on entry (or software clears by writing one) and are remembered while disabled; level-type interrupts fire only while their condition holds. After RETI one instruction of the main program runs before a pending interrupt is served. CLI takes effect at once, even against an interrupt arriving in the same cycle; the instruction after SEI runs before any pending interrupt.

At least five clocks from the interrupt to the first instruction at its vector, during which the program counter is pushed; the usual jump to the handler takes three more. A multi-cycle instruction in progress finishes first. Waking from sleep adds five clocks on top of the sleep mode's start-up time. Returning takes five clocks: the three-byte PC is popped, SP rises by three and I is set.

16 or 32 Kbytes of in-system reprogrammable Flash, organized as 16-bit words (16K x 16 on the 32 Kbyte part) since every instruction is 16 or 32 bits wide, and split into a boot section and an application section for software security. The program counter is 16 bits wide. Constant tables can sit anywhere in program memory and are read with LPM and ELPM.

The first 2,816 data addresses on the 32 Kbyte part cover the 32 registers, 64 I/O registers, 160 extended I/O registers and then 2,560 bytes of SRAM from 0x0100 (to 0x05FF on the 16 Kbyte part, 0x0AFF on the 32 Kbyte part). Five addressing modes reach it: direct (the whole data space), indirect with displacement (63 locations from Y or Z), plain indirect, and indirect with post-increment or pre-decrement. An SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles. No external memory interface is present.

512 bytes or 1 Kbyte of EEPROM in its own data space, read and written a byte at a time, good for at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. A read halts the CPU for four clocks; starting a write halts it for two. A write takes 26,368 cycles of the calibrated RC oscillator, typically 3.3 ms, and hardware clears EEPE when it finishes, so software can poll it. A write needs a timed sequence (EEMPE then EEPE within four cycles), so interrupts should be off for the whole sequence, and a pending SPM must finish first. During a write the EEPROM can neither be read nor have its address changed. The address register is undefined at reset.

At low VCC a write can fail and the CPU can misexecute, both of which corrupt EEPROM data. Holding the part in reset while the supply is too low prevents it: the internal brown-out detector does this, or an external low-VCC reset circuit where the BOD levels do not fit. A write already under way when a reset comes completes, provided the supply is still high enough.

All I/O and peripheral registers sit in I/O space and are reached by LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD. Registers at I/O addresses 0x00 - 0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI and CBI and testable with SBIS and SBIC; IN and OUT use addresses 0x00 - 0x3F, which become 0x20 - 0x5F as data addresses. SBI and CBI touch only the named bit, so they are safe on registers holding flags cleared by writing one. Reserved bits should be written zero and reserved addresses never written. Three general-purpose I/O registers, GPIOR0 to GPIOR2, hold global variables and flags.

Clocks to unused modules can be stopped by the sleep modes. clkCPU runs the core, register file, status register and stack memory. clkI/O runs most I/O modules (timers, SPI, USART) and the external interrupt logic; some external interrupts are detected asynchronously and TWI address recognition works in every sleep mode. clkFLASH runs the Flash interface, normally with clkCPU. clkADC is a separate domain so the CPU and I/O clocks can stop during a conversion for less digital noise. The PLL wants 8 MHz: its prescaler takes an 8 MHz or 16 MHz crystal or external source, dividing by 2 when needed, and its input multiplexer picks that prescaler output or the internal 8 MHz RC oscillator. The PLL runs at a frequency chosen between 32 MHz and 96 MHz, independent of supply voltage, and a postscaler divides it by 1, 1.5 or 2 separately into clkUSB (48 MHz for USB) and clkTMR. clkTMR's maximum depends on supply voltage, reaching 64 MHz at 5 V.

Fuses select a low power crystal oscillator, a low frequency crystal oscillator, the calibrated internal RC oscillator or an external clock. The ATmega16U4 and ATmega32U4 ship with the low power crystal oscillator (8.0 - 16 MHz) and CKDIV8 programmed, giving a 1.0 MHz system clock from an 8 MHz crystal. The RC variants ship with the 8.0 MHz internal RC oscillator and CKDIV8 programmed, also giving 1.0 MHz.

After every other reset source releases, an internal reset holds the part for a time-out tTOUT counted on the watchdog oscillator, chosen by the SUT and CKSEL fuses as 0, 512 or 8K cycles, so that VCC has time to reach a working level. The delay does not watch the voltage, so it must outlast the VCC rise; otherwise a brown-out detector should be used, which also allows the time-out to be turned off (turning it off without a BOD is not advised). A ripple counter then holds reset for a set number of oscillator cycles while the clock settles, ranging from 6 cycles (external clock) up to 32K cycles (32.768 kHz crystal). Waking from Power-save or Power-down counts only the start-up time, since VCC is assumed to be up.

XTAL1 and XTAL2 are the input and output of an inverting amplifier for a quartz crystal or ceramic resonator. It has the lowest power, with a reduced swing on XTAL2, and cannot drive other clock inputs. CKSEL3..1 pick one of four frequency ranges; CKSEL0 with SUT1..0 picks the start-up time. C1 and C2 are always equal.
A dedicated oscillator runs a 32.768 kHz watch crystal, wired as for the low power crystal oscillator. SUT and CKSEL0 select its start-up time of 1K or 32K clocks.

Gives 8.0 MHz nominal at 3 V and 25 °C with no external parts. The factory calibration byte is loaded into OSCCAL during reset, giving 8 MHz ±1% at 3 V and 25 °C; OSCCAL can retune it to anything from 7.3 MHz to 8.1 MHz within ±1%. The watchdog oscillator still clocks the watchdog and the reset time-out. OSCCAL spans ±40% in roughly linear steps of about 0.4%, 0x00 lowest and 0xFF highest; with typical process at 25 °C, 127 gives 8 MHz. Its temperature drift is fairly linear but process dependent; two frequency measurements at two temperatures, using the on-chip sensor, give the slope for temperature compensation. The oscillator also times EEPROM and Flash writes, so it must not be tuned above 8.8 MHz while either is written. RCFREQ in RCCTRL switches the output between 8 MHz (cleared, the default) and 1 MHz, with OSCCAL acting the same way on both.

An outside clock drives XTAL1 with CKSEL set to 0000. The applied frequency must not jump more than 2% from one cycle to the next or behaviour becomes unpredictable; for larger changes hold the part in reset. The system clock prescaler changes the internal frequency at run time safely.

Software can move the system clock between the calibrated 8 MHz RC oscillator, the external clock and the low power crystal oscillator; the low frequency crystal oscillator cannot take part. A typical use is USB suspend: firmware freezes the USB clock, turns off the PLL, starts the RC oscillator, waits for RCON, selects it and turns off the external clock, then sleeps in Power-down with the watchdog as a periodic wake-up. On a resume from the host or an upstream resume from the device it turns the external clock back on, waits for EXTON, selects it, enables the PLL, turns off the RC oscillator, waits for PLOCK and unfreezes the USB clock.

Programming the CKOUT fuse puts the system clock on CLKO (PC7), also during reset, overriding the pin's I/O use. Any clock source can be output, and with the prescaler in use the divided clock comes out.

CLKPR divides the system clock to save power when little processing is needed, with any clock source; clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH are all divided. Switching is glitch-free and no intermediate frequency exceeds either the old or the new one. The prescaler state cannot be read and the exact switch time cannot be predicted. Changing CLKPS takes two writes: CLKPCE set with every other bit zero, then within four cycles the new CLKPS with CLKPCE zero, with interrupts disabled.

The internal PLL makes 32 MHz to 96 MHz from a nominal 8 MHz input for the USB interface and the high-speed timer. Its input comes from a prescaler on the clock source multiplexer, passing an 8 MHz source straight through or halving a 16 MHz one (PINDIV), or from the RC oscillator (PINMUX). Its output passes the postscaler, where USB and the high-speed timer each choose their own division ratio (PLLUSB, PLLTM1:0); PLLE enables it and PLOCK reports lock.

Writing SE in SMCR to one and executing SLEEP enters the mode chosen by SM2..0: 000 Idle, 001 ADC Noise Reduction (ADCNRM), 010 Power-down, 011 Power-save, 110 Standby, 111 Extended Standby. An enabled interrupt wakes the part, which halts four clocks beyond the start-up time, runs the handler and continues after SLEEP, with registers and SRAM unchanged. A reset during sleep wakes it at the reset vector.

Stops clkCPU and clkFLASH only; USB, SPI, USART, analog comparator, ADC, two-wire interface, timers, watchdog and interrupts keep running, so external and internal interrupts (timer overflow, USART transmit complete) wake the part. Setting ACD in ACSR powers down the comparator to save more if it is not needed for wake-up. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

Stops clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH while the ADC, external interrupts, TWI address match and watchdog run, as does clkUSB. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake-up comes from ADC conversion complete, external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, a two-wire interrupt, SPM/EEPROM ready, a level interrupt on INT6, INT3:0 or a pin change.

The external oscillator stops; external interrupts, the two-wire interface and the watchdog keep working. Wake-up comes from external, watchdog or brown-out reset, TWI address match, a level interrupt on INT6, INT3:0, a pin change, or the asynchronous USB interrupts VBUSTI and WAKEUPI. Only asynchronous modules run. A level interrupt used to wake must be held long enough. The wake-up delay is the reset time-out set by the CKSEL fuses.

Power-save equals Power-down on this part, since there is no asynchronous Timer 2; it remains for compatibility with the AT90USB64/128. Standby, with an external crystal or resonator selected, is Power-down with the oscillator left running, and wakes in six clocks. Extended Standby equals Standby for the same reason.

Setting a bit in PRR stops the clock to that peripheral, freezing its state; its registers can then be neither read nor written. Its resources stay taken, so the peripheral is normally disabled first. Clearing the bit brings it back in the state it was left. This saves power in Active and Idle; in the other sleep modes the clocks are stopped anyway.

Use sleep as much as possible and turn off whatever is not needed. An enabled ADC stays on in every sleep mode, and after being turned off and on its next conversion is an extended one. Disable the analog comparator in Idle and ADC Noise Reduction when unused; in other modes it turns off by itself, except when it uses the internal reference, which would then stay on. A BOD enabled by fuses runs in every sleep mode and costs significant current in deep sleep, as does an enabled watchdog. The internal reference is on whenever the BOD, comparator or ADC needs it and must start up before use when turned back on. With the OCDEN fuse programmed, sleep keeps the main clock running; OCD is turned off by unprogramming OCDEN or JTAGEN, or writing JTD in MCUCR.

No pin should drive a resistive load during sleep. In modes where clkI/O and clkADC both stop, the input buffers are turned off except where needed for wake-up. A floating input, or one near VCC/2, draws excess current through an enabled buffer; for analog inputs, disable the digital buffer at all times through DIDR0 and DIDR1.

During reset every I/O register takes its initial value and execution starts at the reset vector, which must hold a JMP to the reset routine. Without enabled interrupts the vector area may hold ordinary code, as it may when the reset vector and interrupt vectors are in different sections. I/O ports return to their initial state as soon as a reset source becomes active, with no clock needed. Once every source releases, a delay counter set by the SUT and CKSEL fuses stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle.

Power-on reset (VCC below VPOT), external reset (RESET low longer than the minimum pulse), watchdog reset (period expired with the watchdog enabled), brown-out reset (VCC below VBOT with the BOD enabled), JTAG AVR reset (while the JTAG reset register holds one), and USB end of reset (if enabled: the CPU resets while the USB controller stays enabled and attached). MCUSR flags the cause: PORF, BORF, EXTRF, WDRF, JTRF, USBRF.

An on-chip detector holds the part in reset whenever VCC is below the detection level; it serves for start-up and to catch supply failures. Crossing the threshold starts the delay counter, which keeps reset active for tTOUT after the VCC rise; reset returns at once when VCC drops below the level. RESET may be tied to VCC or held low externally to extend the start-up.

A low level on RESET longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part, clock or no clock; shorter pulses may not. On the rising edge, once RESET passes VRST, the delay counter starts the part after tTOUT.

The BOD compares VCC with a level set by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis against spikes. When VCC falls below VBOT- the reset is immediate; when it rises above VBOT+ the delay counter starts the part after tTOUT. A dip is caught only if it lasts longer than tBOD.

A watchdog time-out gives a one-CK reset pulse, and tTOUT is counted from its falling edge. With the USB controller enabled and its CPU-reset feature on, a valid USB reset on the bus resets the CPU while the USB controller stays enabled and attached, for better reliability; the bus reset must last at least tUSBRSTMIN, and the CPU restarts at its end.

A bandgap reference feeds the BOD and can feed the analog comparator or the ADC. It is on only while the BOD is enabled by fuse, while ACBG in ACSR connects it to the comparator, or while the ADC is enabled. With the BOD off, it must be given its start-up time after setting ACBG or enabling the ADC before results are used. Avoiding all three conditions turns it off in Power-down.

Counts a separate 128 kHz on-chip oscillator through a prescaler of 2K to 1024K cycles, giving time-outs from 16 ms to 8 s. Modes are interrupt, system reset, and interrupt then system reset (useful to save state before a reset). WDR restarts the count. The interrupt can wake the part from sleep or act as a general timer. The WDTON fuse forces system reset mode with WDE locked at 1 and WDIE at 0. Clearing WDE or changing the period needs a timed sequence: write WDCE and WDE to one together, then within four clocks write WDE and WDP with WDCE clear in one operation. Reset the watchdog before changing WDP, since a shorter period could expire at once. An accidental enable survives the reset it causes, so start-up code should always clear WDRF and WDE.

43 vectors, two words apart from 0x0000: reset, INT0 to INT3, INT6, PCINT0, USB general and endpoint, watchdog, Timer/Counter1 (capture, compare A/B/C, overflow), Timer/Counter0 (compare A/B, overflow), SPI, USART1 (receive, data register empty, transmit), analog comparator, ADC, EEPROM ready, Timer/Counter3 (capture, compare A/B/C, overflow), TWI, SPM ready, and Timer/Counter4 (compare A/B/D, overflow, fault protection).

Every port supports true read-modify-write: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, level or pull-up without touching the others. Outputs drive symmetrically with strong sink and source, enough for LED displays. Each pin has a pull-up whose resistance does not change with supply, and protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has three registers: PORTx (data), DDRx (direction) and PINx (input, read only; writing one to a PINx bit toggles that PORTx bit). PUD in MCUCR turns off every pull-up. Turning on an alternate function on some pins leaves the rest of the port usable as I/O.

DDxn set makes the pin an output, clear an input. On an input, PORTxn set turns on the pull-up. On an output, PORTxn drives the pin high or low. Pins go tri-state at reset, even with no clock. Going between tri-state (00) and output high (11) passes through pull-up on (01) or output low (10); if the pull-up step matters, set PUD. Moving from an input with pull-up to output low, or back, the same applies: step through tri-state or output high.

PINxn reads the pin whatever the direction, through a latch-and-flip-flop synchronizer against metastability, which delays an outside change by between half and one and a half system clocks. Reading back a value just written to PORTx needs a NOP between the OUT and the IN, the delay then being one clock.

In Power-down, Power-save and Standby the sleep controller clamps the digital input to ground ahead of the Schmitt trigger, to avoid current from floating or mid-level inputs. Pins enabled as external interrupts, and some alternate functions, override the clamp. A high level on an asynchronous interrupt pin set for rising, falling or any edge while that interrupt is disabled sets its flag on waking, since the clamp release looks like an edge.

Unused pins should have a defined level to keep current down in reset, active and idle. The internal pull-up is the simplest, but it is off during reset; an external pull-up or pull-down covers reset too. Tying unused pins straight to VCC or GND risks heavy current if a pin is set as an output by mistake.

Alternate functions take over a pin through override signals for the pull-up (PUOE, PUOV), direction (DDOE, DDOV), output value (PVOE, PVOV), output toggle (PTOE) and digital input enable (DIEOE, DIEOV), and receive the pin through DI (digital, after the Schmitt trigger) or AIO (analog, straight to the pad).

PB7 is OC0A, OC1C (timer compare outputs, also their PWM outputs, with DDB7 set), PCINT7 and USART RTS. PB6 is OC1B, PCINT6, OC4B (high-speed PWM, DDB6 set) and ADC13. PB5 is OC1A, PCINT5, the complement of OC4B, and ADC12. PB4 is PCINT4 and ADC11. PB3 is PDO for serial programming, MISO (forced input as SPI master, DDB3 controls it as slave) and PCINT3. PB2 is PDI, MOSI (forced input as slave, DDB2 controls it as master) and PCINT2. PB1 is SCK (forced input as slave) and PCINT1. PB0 is SS (forced input as slave, where a low level activates the SPI) and PCINT0. Where the SPI forces a pin to input, PORTBn still controls its pull-up.

PC7 is ICP3 (Timer/Counter3 input capture), CLKO (system clock when the CKOUT fuse is programmed, after the prescaler) and OC4A (high-speed PWM, DDC7 set). PC6 is OC3A (Timer/Counter3 PWM) and the complement of OC4A (DDC6 set).

PD7 is T0 (Timer/Counter0 clock), OC4D (high-speed PWM, DDD7 set) and ADC10. PD6 is T1, the complement of OC4D (DDD6 set) and ADC9. PD5 is XCK1 (USART1 clock, output when DDD5 is set, active only in synchronous mode) and CTS. PD4 is ICP1 and ADC8. PD3 is INT3 and TXD1, an output whenever the transmitter is on. PD2 is INT2 and RXD1, an input whenever the receiver is on, with PORTD2 still controlling the pull-up. PD1 is INT1 and SDA; PD0 is INT0, SCL and OC0B. With TWEN set, PD0 and PD1 leave the port and become the two-wire pins, with a 50 ns spike filter on the input and an open-drain, slew-rate-limited driver.

PE6 is INT6 and AIN0, wired straight to the analog comparator. PE2 is H̅W̅B̅: with the HWBE fuse programmed, holding it low during an external reset starts the boot loader section after reset; otherwise it is an ordinary I/O pin.

Port F pins are ADC inputs; a port F pin used as an output must not switch during a conversion, or the result may be corrupted. PF7 is ADC7 and TDI, PF6 ADC6 and TDO (tri-stated except while the TAP shifts data out), PF5 ADC5 and TMS, PF4 ADC4 and TCK; with JTAG enabled these four cannot be used as I/O, and the TDI, TMS and TCK pull-ups stay on even through reset. PF1 and PF0 are ADC1 and ADC0.

INT6, INT3:0 and PCINT7..0 raise interrupts even when the pins are outputs, which allows software interrupts. PCI0 fires when any enabled PCINT7:0 pin toggles; PCMSK0 picks the pins. Pin change interrupts, low-level interrupts and the edge interrupts on INT3:0 are detected asynchronously and can wake the part from any sleep mode; rising or falling edge detection on INT6 needs the I/O clock, which runs only in Idle. EICRA (INT3:0) and EICRB (INT6) choose falling edge, rising edge or low level; a level interrupt keeps firing while the pin is low. For a level wake-up from Power-down, the level must last until the start-up time ends, or the part wakes without taking the interrupt.
Timer/Counter0, 1 and 3 share one prescaler, each with its own clock select. A timer runs straight from the system clock (CSn2:0 = 1, up to fCLK_I/O) or from a tap at fCLK_I/O/8, /64, /256 or /1024.

The prescaler runs free of the timers' clock select. So when a timer is started on a prescaled clock, its first count comes 1 to N+1 system clocks later, N being the divisor (8, 64, 256 or 1024). Resetting the prescaler lines a timer up with program flow, but it shifts the prescaled period of every timer sharing it.

A clock on the Tn pin is sampled every system clock by a synchronizer followed by an edge detector; CSn2:0 = 7 counts rising edges, 6 falling. An edge reaches the counter 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks after it arrives. Tn should be steady for at least one system clock while the input is switched on or off, or a false count can occur. Each half period must exceed one system clock. An external clock cannot be prescaled. T3 is not brought out on this part, so Tn means T0 or T1.

Setting TSM in GTCCR holds whatever is written to PSRASY and PSRSYNC, keeping the prescaler resets asserted so the timers can be set to the same value without one moving. Clearing TSM lets hardware clear those bits and the timers start together. PSRSYNC resets the prescaler shared by Timer/Counter0, 1 and 3 and is normally cleared by hardware at once.

An 8-bit timer/counter with two output compare units, double-buffered compare registers, auto-reload on compare match (CTC), phase correct PWM free of glitches, variable PWM period, a frequency generator and three interrupt sources: TOV0, OCF0A and OCF0B. TCNT0, OCR0A and OCR0B are 8-bit; flags sit in TIFR0 and masks in TIMSK0. It counts the prescaled internal clock or the T0 pin, and stops when no clock is selected (CS02:0 = 0).

Each timer clock the counter is cleared, incremented or decremented, as set by WGM01:0 in TCCR0A and WGM02 in TCCR0B. The CPU can read or write TCNT0 with or without a clock, and its write wins over any count or clear in that cycle. TOV0 is set as the mode decides and can raise an interrupt.

TCNT0 is compared with OCR0A and OCR0B all the time; a match sets OCF0A or OCF0B on the next timer clock, which raises an interrupt if enabled and clears itself when the interrupt runs, or is cleared by writing it one. In the PWM modes OCR0x is double buffered and updates at TOP or BOTTOM, so pulses never come out odd-length; in Normal and CTC modes the CPU writes OCR0x straight.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter0 force compare and TCNT0 writes
operation.text: In non-PWM modes writing FOC0x acts on OC0x as a real match would, without setting OCF0x or clearing the timer. Any CPU write to TCNT0 blocks a match in the next timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so OCR0x can equal TCNT0 at start without an interrupt. Writing TCNT0 equal to OCR0x therefore loses that match, and writing BOTTOM while counting down is to be avoided. OC0x should be set up, for instance with FOC0x in Normal mode, before the pin's DDR bit is made an output; OC0x keeps its state across mode changes, and COM0x1:0 changes take effect at once, not buffered with the compare value.

COM0x1:0 sets what the next match does to the OC0x register and whether OC0x drives the pin in place of the port. The pin shows OC0x only with its DDR bit set as output. A system reset clears OC0x. COM0x1:0 = 0 means no action at the next match; a change of COM0x1:0 acts at the next match, or at once in non-PWM modes when forced with FOC0x.

WGM02:0 = 0: the counter only counts up and rolls over from 0xFF to 0x00, setting TOV0 in the cycle it reaches zero. TOV0 acts like a ninth bit that is only ever set, so software with the overflow interrupt can extend the count. The counter can be written at any time. Compare matches can time interrupts, but making waveforms this way costs too much CPU time.

WGM02:0 = 2: the counter clears when it equals OCR0A, so OCR0A sets TOP and the resolution. OCF0A can interrupt at each TOP to load a new TOP, but CTC has no double buffering: a new OCR0A below the present TCNT0 misses the match and the counter runs to 0xFF and wraps first. With COM0A1:0 = 1 OC0A toggles each match, up to fclk_I/O/2 at OCR0A = 0. TOV0 is set when the count passes from MAX to 0x00.

WGM02:0 = 3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 7 (TOP = OCR0A): single slope from BOTTOM to TOP, then back to BOTTOM, giving up to twice the frequency of phase correct mode. COM0x1:0 = 2 clears OC0x at the match and sets it at BOTTOM (non-inverted); 3 inverts this. COM0A1:0 = 1 toggles OC0A on matches only when WGM02 is set; OC0B has no toggle. TOV0 is set at each TOP. OCR0A = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks; OCR0A = MAX gives a steady high or low. Toggling with OCR0A = 0 gives a 50% square wave of up to fclk_I/O/2, like CTC but with the buffer on.

WGM02:0 = 1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 5 (TOP = OCR0A): dual slope, up from BOTTOM to TOP and back, holding TOP for one timer clock. Non-inverted, OC0x clears on the match counting up and sets on the match counting down; COM0x1:0 = 3 inverts. COM0A0 = 1 toggles OC0A when WGM02 is set; not on OC0B. Being symmetric, these modes are preferred for motor control. TOV0 is set at BOTTOM. OCR0A at BOTTOM gives a steady low, at MAX a steady high (non-inverted).

In phase correct mode OCnx can change at BOTTOM with no match, to keep the waveform symmetric about BOTTOM. This happens when OCR0A moves away from MAX, and when the timer starts above OCR0A and so misses the up-count match.

The timer is fully synchronous; clkT0 acts as a clock enable. TOV0 is set as TCNT0 goes from MAX to BOTTOM; OCF0x is set on the timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x; in CTC and in fast PWM with TOP = OCR0A, OCF0A is set and TCNT0 cleared as the count passes TOP.

Two 16-bit timer/counters for event timing, waveforms and signal measurement: true 16-bit PWM, three output compare units (A, B, C) with double-buffered registers, one input capture unit with noise canceler, clear on compare match, glitch-free phase correct PWM, variable period, frequency generator, external event counter, and ten interrupt sources (TOV1, OCF1A, OCF1B, OCF1C, ICF1 and the same for timer 3). PRTIM1 in PRR0 and PRTIM3 in PRR1 must be 0 to run them. T3 is not brought out, so only Timer/Counter1 has an external clock pin (T1).

TOP can be OCRnA, ICRn or a fixed value. With OCRnA as TOP in a PWM mode, OCRnA cannot also drive a PWM output, but TOP is then double buffered and can change at run time; ICRn as TOP leaves OCRnA free for PWM.

The 16-bit TCNTn, OCRnA/B/C and ICRn registers are reached as two bytes through one shared 8-bit TEMP register per timer. The low byte access triggers the 16-bit transfer: writing the low byte copies TEMP into the high byte in the same clock, and reading the low byte copies the high byte into TEMP. Write high byte first; read low byte first. Reading OCRnA/B/C does not use TEMP. A C compiler handles the order itself. When the same high byte goes to several registers it needs writing only once.

A 16-bit access takes two instructions. If an interrupt between them touches TEMP through any 16-bit register of that timer, the outer access is corrupted, so main code that shares TEMP with an interrupt must disable interrupts across the access (save SREG, CLI, access, restore SREG).

TCNTnH is reached only through TEMP: it loads TEMP when TCNTnL is read and takes TEMP when TCNTnL is written, so the whole count moves in one clock. Writing TCNTn while counting can give unpredictable results in some cases. The count sequence follows WGMn3:0 in TCCRnA and TCCRnB; CSn2:0 = 0 stops the timer, and a CPU write wins over counting.

An event on ICPn, or for Timer/Counter1 only on the analog comparator output, copies TCNTn into ICRn and sets ICFn in the same system clock; with TICIEn set an interrupt follows, which clears ICFn, or software writes ICFn one. Read ICRnL before ICRnH. ICRn can be written only in modes that use it as TOP, with WGMn3:0 set first and the high byte written first. Setting ACIC in ACSR picks the comparator as source; switching source can itself trigger a capture, so clear ICFn afterwards.

operation.topic: Input capture sampling and noise canceler
operation.text: ICPn and the comparator output are sampled like the Tn pin and use the same edge detector. The noise canceler, enabled by ICNCn in TCCRnB, needs four equal samples in a row before the output changes, adding four system clocks of delay; it runs on the system clock, not the prescaler. The capture input is active unless the mode uses ICRn as TOP. Software can trigger a capture by driving the ICPn port bit.

ICRn is overwritten by the next event if not read in time, so read it early in the interrupt; the worst-case interrupt latency depends on the longest other handler. Capturing while TOP changes at run time is not recommended. For duty cycle, change the edge right after reading ICRn and then clear ICFn; frequency alone needs no flag clearing when an interrupt is used. In Normal mode the time between events must fit in the counter, or the overflow interrupt or prescaler extends it.

TCNTn is compared with each OCRnx all the time; a match sets OCFnx on the next timer clock and raises an interrupt when OCIEnx is set. Unit A can also set TOP, which fixes the waveform period. OCRnx is double buffered in all twelve PWM modes and updated at TOP or BOTTOM; in Normal and CTC modes the CPU writes it directly. The timer never changes OCRnx itself, so reading it does not use TEMP, but writing it does: high byte first, then the low byte moves both into the buffer or compare register in the same clock.

In non-PWM modes FOCnx forces the match action on OCnx without setting OCFnx or clearing the timer. A write to TCNTn blocks any match in the next timer clock, even when stopped. Writing TCNTn equal to OCRnx loses that match; writing TOP in a PWM mode with variable TOP skips TOP and the counter runs to 0xFFFF; writing BOTTOM while counting down is to be avoided. Set up OCnx (for instance with FOCnx in Normal mode) before making the pin an output; OCnx keeps its state across mode changes, and COMnx1:0 changes act at once.

COMnx1:0 sets the next match's action on OCnx and connects OCnx to the pin in place of the port, the pin direction still coming from its DDR bit, which must be an output to show OCnx. Reset clears OCnx. COMnx1:0 = 0 means no action; a change acts at the next match, or at once with FOCnx in non-PWM modes. COMnx1:0 does not affect input capture.
WGMn3:0 = 0: count up only, roll over from 0xFFFF to 0x0000, set TOVn in the cycle it reaches zero. TOVn acts like a 17th bit that is only set; the counter can be written at any time.

WGMn3:0 = 4 clears the counter on a match with OCRnA, 12 on a match with ICRn; OCFnA or ICFn can interrupt at each TOP. With no double buffering, a new TOP below the present count misses the match and the counter runs to 0xFFFF and wraps first; fast PWM with OCRnA as TOP (WGMn3:0 = 15) avoids this, as OCRnA is then buffered. COMnA1:0 = 1 toggles OCnA each match, up to fclk_I/O/2 at OCRnA = 0x0000. TOVn is set as the count passes MAX to 0x0000.

WGMn3:0 = 5, 6 or 7 count up to fixed TOPs of 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF (8, 9 or 10 bits); 14 uses ICRn and 15 OCRnA as TOP, from 2-bit (0x0003) up to 16-bit. Single slope, then clear on the next timer clock. Non-inverted (COMnx1:0 = 2), OCnx is set at the match and cleared at TOP; 3 inverts. TOVn is set at TOP, together with OCFnA or ICFn when that register is TOP. A new TOP must not be below any compare register, or no match occurs; with fixed TOPs the unused bits of OCRnx are masked to zero on writing. ICRn is not double buffered, so a low ICRn written while running may be passed and the counter wraps at 0xFFFF; OCRnA is buffered and loads at TOP, making it the better TOP when the period changes. OCRnx = BOTTOM gives a spike every TOP+1 clocks; OCRnx = TOP a steady level. With OCR1A as TOP (WGM13:0 = 15) and COMnA1:0 = 1, OCnA gives a 50% square wave up to fclk_I/O/2.

WGMn3:0 = 1, 2 or 3 use fixed TOPs of 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF; 10 uses ICRn and 11 OCRnA. Dual slope, holding TOP for one timer clock. Non-inverted, OCnx clears on the up-count match and sets on the down-count match. TOVn is set at BOTTOM; OCFnA or ICFn is set at TOP when OCRnx loads from its buffer. Because OCRnx updates at TOP, changing TOP while running makes the two slopes of a period differ in length and the output asymmetric; phase and frequency correct mode is recommended when TOP changes. OCRnx = BOTTOM gives steady low, TOP steady high (non-inverted). With OCR1A as TOP (WGM13:0 = 11) and COM1A1:0 = 1, OC1A toggles at 50% duty.

WGMn3:0 = 8 (TOP = ICRn) or 9 (TOP = OCRnA), 2-bit to 16-bit. Dual slope like phase correct mode, but OCRnx loads from its buffer at BOTTOM, so both slopes of every period are equal and the output stays symmetric. TOVn is set at BOTTOM, OCFnA or ICFn at TOP. A new TOP must not fall below any compare value. OCRnx = BOTTOM gives a steady low, TOP a high (non-inverted). With OCR1A as TOP (WGM13:0 = 9) and COM1A1:0 = 1, OC1A toggles at 50% duty.

OCFnx is set on the timer clock after TCNTn equals OCRnx. In CTC and fast PWM the count passes TOP to BOTTOM; in the dual-slope modes it turns at TOP. TOVn (fast PWM) and ICFn (when TOP) are set at TOP, where OCRnx takes its new value; in phase and frequency correct mode the update happens at BOTTOM instead.

A high-speed timer/counter of up to 10 bits with three output compare units (A, B, D) and OCR4C as TOP, clear on compare match, glitch-free phase and frequency correct PWM, an enhanced PWM mode that adds one bit of resolution at the same output frequency, variable period, a dead-time generator per PWM channel, synchronous update of the PWM registers, five interrupt sources (TOV4, OCF4A, OCF4B, OCF4D, FPF4), asynchronous and synchronous clocking and its own prescaler. It can drive three PWM outputs at clocks up to 64 MHz, each with non-overlapping true and inverted outputs.
The timer runs up to 64 MHz; below a 4 V supply a lower input frequency is recommended, as the timer is slower at low voltage.

The registers are 8-bit with a shared 2-bit high byte register, TC4H, carrying the two MSBs of each 10-bit value; with those MSBs written 0 the timer works as an 8-bit timer. Reading a low byte loads its two MSBs into TC4H; writing a low byte takes them from TC4H. In enhanced mode TC4H holds one more bit, the MSB of an 11-bit compare value.

TCNT4 and OCR4A, OCR4B, OCR4C and OCR4D are compared registers; OCR4A, OCR4B and OCR4D act on the OC4A, OC4B and OC4D pins and raise compare interrupts, while OCR4C holds TOP. Flags are in TIFR4 and TCCR4D (FPF4), masks in TIMSK4 and FPIE4 in TCCR4D; control is in TCCR4A to TCCR4E.

In asynchronous mode the timer and its prescaler run on the fast peripheral clock PCK (up to 64 MHz) across a synchronization boundary, while the CPU runs from any clock. Register writes pass through input synchronizers before acting. TCCR4A to D and OCR4A to D read back at once after a write; TCNT4, TC4H and the flags OCF4A, OCF4B, OCF4D and TOV4 read back delayed. The system clock must be below half the PCK frequency, since synchronization needs two PCK edges while the system clock is high; otherwise data or control values can be lost.

The counter is cleared, incremented or decremented each clkT4, taken from the system clock or the asynchronous PLL clock by CS4<3:0> and the PLL postscaler bits PLLTM1:0. CS4<3:0> = 0 stops it; TCNT4 stays accessible and a CPU write wins. The sequence follows PWM4x and WGM40 in TCCR4A, TCCR4C and TCCR4D, which also decide when TOV4 is set.
To switch to asynchronous mode: enable the PLL, wait 100 µs for it to settle, poll PLOCK until set, then set PLLTM1:0 in PLLFRQ to a value other than 0:0.

A match of TCNT4 with OCR4A, OCR4B or OCR4D sets OCF4x on the next timer clock and can interrupt; the flag clears when the interrupt runs or by writing one. The waveform generator acts on the match as PWM4x, WGM40 and COM4x1:0 set. OCR4x is double buffered in the PWM modes, updating at TOP or BOTTOM to keep pulses glitch-free; between write and update a read returns the newest written value. Normal mode has no buffering.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter4 force compare and TCNT4 writes
operation.text: In non-PWM modes FOC4x updates OCW4x as a real match would, without setting OCF4x or clearing the timer. A TCNT4 write blocks a match in the next timer clock, even when stopped; writing TCNT4 equal to OCR4x loses that match, and writing BOTTOM while counting down is to be avoided. Set up OCW4x, for instance with FOC4x in Normal mode, before making the pin an output; COM4x1:0 changes act at once.

In PWM modes with COM4x1:0 = 01, each of the three channels turns its waveform OCW4x into a complementary pair OC4x and O̅C̅4̅x̅ with dead time between them, for driving external power switches safely. A 4-bit down counter, loaded from DT4H on one edge of OCW4x and from DT4L on the other, delays the rising edge of the output it applies to; DT4H sets the non-overlap time at the rising edge and DT4L at the falling edge, in prescaled clocks. Its own prescaler, set by DTPS41:40, splits PCK or CK down by a factor of 1, 2, 4 or 8. With zero dead time the outputs still lag OCW4x by at least one timer clock. Setting PWM4X inverts both outputs, which then are both high during the dead time.

COM4x1:0 decides the non-inverted or inverted OCW4x at the next match and routes OC4x and O̅C̅4̅x̅ to the pins. In Normal mode the dead-time block only synchronizes, delaying OC4x one timer clock from OCW4x. In fast PWM and phase and frequency correct PWM with COM4x1:0 = 01 both outputs are made with programmable dead time; other settings behave as in Normal mode. Reset clears OC4x. The pins show the outputs only with their DDR bits set as outputs.

Setting ENHC4 in TCCR4E adds an accuracy bit to OCR4A, OCR4B and OCR4D: the value written is shifted right by one, and its LSB picks whether the match is signalled on the normal clock edge (0) or the next, opposite edge (1). The PWM frequency is unchanged and resolution improves, to at most 11 bits; TC4H may then be 3 bits wide for these registers. OCR4C, which sets the period, takes no extra bit. Example: with a 64 MHz PLL postscaler output and no prescaling, OCR4C = 0x7F gives 7-bit resolution at 500 kHz; OCR4A = 0x85 means a compare value of 0x42 plus the extra bit, a duty cycle of 51.95%, between the 51.56% and 52.34% of 0x42 and 0x43.

Each compare register write normally takes effect only when the running PWM cycle ends, so several registers written at high PWM rates may not change together. With TLOCK4 = 1 written values are held in buffers; clearing TLOCK4 loads the whole new set together once the running PWM cycle ends.

PWM4x = 0: the counter counts from BOTTOM to TOP (OCR4C) and restarts, so OCR4C sets resolution and match frequency. Toggle mode toggles OCW4x on a match, non-inverting clears it, inverting sets it. TOV4 is set as TCNT4 reaches zero and acts like an 11th bit that is only set. Toggling OCW4x (COM4x1:0 = 1) gives up to fclkT4/4 at OCR4C = 0, but waveforms in Normal mode cost much CPU time.

PWM4x = 1, WGM40 = 0: single slope from BOTTOM to TOP (OCR4C), then cleared. Non-inverting clears OCW4x at the match and sets it at BOTTOM; inverting does the opposite; COM4x1:0 = 1 is complementary mode, giving both OC4x and O̅C̅4̅x̅. TOV4 is set at each TOP. OCR4C = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 clocks; OCR4C = MAX a steady level. Toggling gives a 50% wave up to fclkT4/4 with OCR4C = 3. The port is overridden only while COM4x1:0 is non-zero and the pins are outputs.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter4 phase and frequency correct PWM
operation.text: PWM4x = 1, WGM40 = 1: dual slope between BOTTOM and TOP (OCR4C), holding TOP one timer clock. Non-inverting and complementary modes clear OCW4x on the up-count match and set it on the down-count match; inverting is the reverse; COM4x1:0 = 1 gives both outputs. TOV4 is set at BOTTOM. OCR4C = BOTTOM gives a steady low, MAX a steady high (non-inverted).

PWM4A = 1 and WGM41 = 1 select PWM6 mode for brushless DC motor drive: OCR4A alone sets all six outputs, all made from OCW4A, and the override enable register OC4OE switches each pin between the waveform and its port bit at once. WGM40 = 0 counts single slope (like fast PWM, TOV4 at TOP); WGM40 = 1 dual slope (like phase and frequency correct PWM, TOV4 at BOTTOM).

clkT4 acts as a clock enable. TOV4 is set as TCNT4 passes TOP to BOTTOM in all modes but phase and frequency correct, where it is set at BOTTOM; OCF4x is set on the timer clock after TCNT4 equals OCR4x.

With FPEN4 set, an event on INT0, or on the analog comparator output when FPAC4 in TCCR4D is set, that matches the edge setting clears the COM4x bits, disconnects the compare outputs and puts the port register bits back on the PWM pins. FPEN4 clears in the same system clock; with FPIE4 set a fault interrupt follows, otherwise software can poll FPEN4. Changing the source, the edge setting or enabling protection can itself trigger it, so clearing FPF4 afterwards is recommended. The inputs are sampled like T0; the noise canceler (FPNC4) needs four equal samples and adds four system clocks of delay, independent of the prescaler. Software can trigger it by driving the INT0 port bit.

10-bit values in TCNT4 and OCR4A/B/C/D move through the shared TC4H register: write TC4H before the low byte, read the low byte before TC4H. The low byte access copies TC4H in or out in the same clock. An interrupt touching TC4H between the two instructions corrupts the outer access, so main code sharing TC4H with interrupts must disable them across it. A high byte common to several registers needs writing only once.

Output compare unit C of Timer/Counter1 and unit A of Timer/Counter0 share pin PB7. Either one, when its COMnx1:0 is non-zero, takes over from PORTB7; with both enabled the modulator switches on by itself and combines them. PORTB7 = 0 gives logical AND, PORTB7 = 1 logical OR. DDRB7 sets the pin direction whatever the COM bits.

With Timer/Counter0 as the carrier (CTC, toggle) and OC1C as the modulating fast PWM signal, the PWM resolution drops by the number of system clocks in one carrier period, since high times that differ by less than that come out the same on PB7.

A full-duplex, three-wire synchronous serial port, master or slave, LSB or MSB first, seven bit rates (the clock divided by 2 to 128), an end-of-transfer flag, write collision protection, wake-up from Idle, and double-speed (CK/2) master mode. The USART can also act as an SPI master. PRSPI in PRR0 must be 0 to use it.

The master pulls the slave's S̅S̅ low, both sides load their shift registers, and the master clocks SCK; data goes out on MOSI and comes back on MISO at the same time. The master has no automatic S̅S̅ control: software drives it. Writing SPDR starts the clock; after eight bits the clock stops and SPIF is set, raising an interrupt when SPIE is set. The master writes the next byte or raises S̅S̅ to end the packet; the last received byte stays in the buffer.

While S̅S̅ is high the slave sleeps with MISO tri-stated; SPDR can be loaded but no data shifts out. With S̅S̅ low it shifts on SCK, sets SPIF after each byte and can interrupt. Transmit is single buffered: a new byte cannot be written until the shift completes. Receive is double buffered: a byte must be read before the next has fully arrived or it is lost. The slave samples SCK, which must stay at or below fosc/4.

As a slave, S̅S̅ is always an input. Low activates the SPI and lets MISO drive if set as output; high makes all pins inputs, stops reception, resets the SPI logic and drops any partly received byte, which keeps the slave's bit counter in step with the master.

As master (MSTR set) the direction of S̅S̅ is the user's choice. As an output it is a plain port pin, typically driving a slave's S̅S̅. As an input it must stay high; if pulled low, the SPI takes it as another master selecting it: MSTR clears, the part becomes a slave with MOSI and SCK as inputs, and SPIF is set, interrupting if enabled. Interrupt-driven masters should therefore check that MSTR is still set, and set it again if a slave select cleared it.
CPOL and CPHA give four combinations of clock polarity and phase; data are shifted out on one SCK edge and latched on the opposite one, leaving time to settle. DORD = 0 sends MSB first, 1 LSB first.

A full-duplex universal synchronous and asynchronous receiver and transmitter: asynchronous or clocked synchronous (master or slave), C̅T̅S̅/R̅T̅S̅ hardware flow control, a high-resolution baud rate generator, frames of 5 to 9 data bits with 1 or 2 stop bits, hardware odd or even parity, overrun and framing error detection, noise filtering with false start-bit rejection and a digital low-pass filter, separate interrupts for transmit complete, empty transmit data register and receive complete, a multi-processor mode and double-speed asynchronous mode.

The USART has a clock generator, a transmitter and a receiver sharing the control registers. The clock generator holds the baud rate generator and a synchronizer for an external XCKn clock, used only in synchronous mode. The transmitter has a single write buffer, so frames can follow without gaps, a shift register, parity generator and frame control. The receiver adds clock and data recovery for asynchronous input, a parity checker, its own shift register and a receive buffer two levels deep (UDRn), and detects frame, overrun and parity errors.

Four clock modes: asynchronous at normal or double speed, and synchronous as master or as slave. UMSELn in UCSRnC picks asynchronous or synchronous; U2Xn in UCSRnA picks double speed (asynchronous only). In synchronous mode the DDR bit of XCKn picks an internal clock (master, output) or external clock (slave, input).

A down counter on the system clock reloads from UBRRn each time it reaches zero, or when UBRRLn is written, and gives a clock pulse at fosc/(UBRRn+1). The transmitter divides this by 2, 8 or 16 according to mode; the receiver's recovery units use it directly with a state machine of 2, 8 or 16 states set by UMSELn, U2Xn and the XCKn DDR bit.

U2Xn = 1 halves the baud divider from 16 to 8 in asynchronous mode, doubling the rate; it should be 0 in synchronous mode. The receiver then takes only 8 samples per bit, so baud rate and system clock must be more accurate; the transmitter is not affected.
In synchronous slave mode the XCKn input passes a synchronization register and an edge detector, which adds two CPU clocks of delay and limits XCKn to below fOSC/4.

In synchronous mode XCKn is clock input (slave) or output (master). Data are sampled on RxDn at the opposite XCKn edge from the one where TxDn changes: with UCPOLn = 0 data change on the rising edge and are sampled on the falling edge; UCPOLn = 1 reverses this.

A frame is one start bit (low), 5 to 9 data bits LSB first, an optional even or odd parity bit, and 1 or 2 stop bits (high): 30 valid combinations. Frames can follow each other directly or the line idles high. UCSZn2:0 sets the data bits, UPMn1:0 the parity and USBSn the stop bits, shared by receiver and transmitter; changing them corrupts any transfer in progress. The receiver ignores the second stop bit, so a frame error is flagged only when the first stop bit is 0.
The parity bit is the exclusive-or of the data bits, inverted for odd parity, and is placed after the final data bit, ahead of the stop bits.

Set the baud rate, the frame format, and enable transmitter and/or receiver; for interrupt-driven use, interrupts should be off while doing so. Before changing baud rate or frame format, make sure nothing is being sent or received: TXCn shows the transmitter has finished (clear it before each UDRn write if used this way) and RXCn shows unread data.

TXENn in UCSRnB takes over the TxDn pin as serial output; in synchronous mode the XCKn clock drives transmission. Writing UDRn loads the transmit buffer, which passes to the shift register as soon as that is idle, or straight after the preceding frame's final stop bit. In frames under 8 bits the unused upper bits written to UDRn are ignored. For 9-bit frames (UCSZn = 7) the ninth bit goes into TXB8n in UCSRnB before the low byte is written to UDRn; it can mark address frames in multi-processor mode.

UDREn is set while the transmit buffer is empty and cleared by writing UDRn; with UDRIEn set its interrupt keeps running while UDREn is set, so the handler must write UDRn or turn the interrupt off. TXCn is set when the whole frame has left the shift register and no new data waits; it clears when its interrupt (TXCIEn) runs or by writing one, and suits half-duplex buses such as RS-485 that must release the line after sending. Write UDREn as 0 when writing UCSRnA.
With UPMn1 = 1 the transmitter inserts the parity bit before the first stop bit. Clearing TXENn takes effect only after the shift register and buffer have emptied; the pin then returns to the port.

RXENn takes over RxDn as serial input. Reception starts on a valid start bit; each bit is sampled on the baud clock (or XCKn) up to the first stop bit, a second being ignored, and the frame then moves to the receive buffer read through UDRn. In frames under 8 bits the unused upper bits read as 0. For 9-bit frames read RXB8n in UCSRnB first, and read FEn, DORn and UPEn in UCSRnA before UDRn, since reading UDRn moves the buffer on and changes them.

RXCn is set while unread data are in the receive buffer; disabling the receiver flushes the buffer and clears RXCn. With RXCIEn set the receive interrupt keeps running while RXCn is set, so the handler must read UDRn.

FEn, DORn and UPEn are stored with their frame in the receive buffer, so UCSRnA must be read before UDRn; software cannot set them and none raises an interrupt; write them as 0 when writing UCSRnA. FEn is 1 when the next frame to be read had a 0 in its first stop bit, which helps detect lost sync and break conditions. DORn shows that a frame was lost because the buffer (two characters) and the shift register were full when another start bit came; it clears when a frame moves into the buffer. UPEn shows a parity error in the next frame when parity checking was on, and is always 0 with checking off.
UPMn1 enables checking and UPMn0 selects odd or even. The check result is stored with the frame and read as UPEn, valid until UDRn is read.
Clearing RXENn takes effect at once: a frame in progress and any data in the buffer are lost, and RxDn returns to the port. To flush the buffer while running, read UDRn until RXCn clears.

The receiver samples at 16 times the baud rate (8 in double speed). A high-to-low edge on idle RxDn starts start-bit detection: samples 8, 9 and 10 (4, 5 and 6 in double speed) are voted, and if two or more are high the edge is rejected as a spike. A valid start bit synchronizes the recovery, and this repeats for every frame.

Each bit is decided by a majority vote of the three centre samples (16 states per bit, 8 in double speed), acting as a low-pass filter. The stop bit is voted the same way; a 0 sets FEn. Only the first stop bit is used. The next start edge may come right after the voting samples of the stop bit, earlier in normal speed than in double speed, which affects the operational range.

Reception fails if the incoming bit rate differs too much from the internal baud rate. Normal speed tolerates more variation than double speed. Error comes from the receiver's system clock, which with a resonator can differ by more than 2%, and from the baud generator not dividing exactly; a UBRR value with low error should be chosen.

With MPCMn set the receiver drops frames that carry no address. With 5 to 8 data bits the first stop bit marks an address frame (1) or data frame (0); with 9 data bits RXB8n does. The master sends 9-bit frames with TXB8n = 1 for an address. Each slave in MPCMn mode reads the address frame; the one addressed clears MPCMn and takes the data frames that follow, while the rest ignore them until the next address frame; after the last data frame the addressed slave sets MPCMn again. 5 to 8-bit frames are possible but awkward, needing two stop bits on the transmitter. MPCMn shares its I/O location with TXCn, so SBI and CBI must not be used on it.

With RTSEN in UCSRnD set, the R̅T̅S̅ pin tells the remote transmitter when the receive FIFO is full. R̅T̅S̅ rises at two thirds of the last received stop bit when the FIFO is full; one more byte can still be taken into the receive shift register should the transmitter miss the signal.
With CTSEN in UCSRnD set, the transmitter stops while the remote receiver holds C̅T̅S̅ high (full). C̅T̅S̅ is sampled at each CPU write and in the middle of the last stop bit being sent.

With common crystal and resonator frequencies most standard baud rates are reached within a small error. Errors above 0.5% are usable but lower the receiver's noise margin, especially with long frames.

Setting both UMSELn1:0 bits makes the USART an SPI master (MSPIM): full duplex three-wire transfer, all four SPI modes, MSB or LSB first, double-buffered queued operation, the high-resolution baud generator, up to fXCK = fCK/2, and flexible interrupts. The SPI logic takes over the shift registers, buffers and baud generator; parity, clock and data recovery and the RX/TX control are disabled; pin control and interrupts are as in USART mode. The register locations are the same, with some bits changing meaning.
Only master operation exists, so the XCKn DDR bit must be 1 (output), preferably before TXENn and RXENn are set. Clock generation is that of synchronous master mode.

UCPHAn and UCPOLn give the four clock phase and polarity combinations; data shift out and latch on opposite XCKn edges. A frame is 8 data bits, MSB or LSB first as UDORDn in UCSRnC sets, shared by receiver and transmitter. Changing these bits corrupts a transfer in progress. Writing two bytes to UDRn sends 16 bits, with the transmit complete interrupt at the end.

Set the baud rate, make XCKn an output, set the frame format and enable transmitter and receiver; only the transmitter can work alone. For XCKn to start at once, UBRRn must be 0 when the transmitter is enabled and be given its value afterwards, before the first transfer; after reset UBRRn is already 0. Before changing baud rate, data mode or format, check with TXCn and RXCn that nothing is in progress.

The transmitter must be enabled; it takes over TxDn. Enabling the receiver is optional and takes over RxDn; XCKn is the transfer clock either way. Writing UDRn starts every transfer, receive included, since the transmitter makes the clock. UDRn must be read once per byte sent to keep the receive buffer in step: on overflow the newest byte is lost, so after four transfers with no reads the third byte is the one dropped. RXCn, TXCn and UDREn behave as in USART mode; FE, DOR and PE are unused and read 0. Disabling works as in USART mode.

MSPIM matches the SPI master timing, and UCPOLn, UCPHAn and UDORDn act like CPOL, CPHA and DORD. It differs in having a buffered transmitter (the SPI has none) and an extra receive buffer level, no WCOL bit, no SPI2X bit (the same is reached through UBRRn), incompatible interrupt timing, master-only operation and different pin control.

A two-line (SCL clock, SDA data) bus interface: master and slave, transmitter or receiver, 7-bit addresses for up to 128 slaves, multi-master arbitration, up to 400 kHz, slew-rate limited outputs, spike suppression on the inputs, a fully programmable slave address with general call, and wake-up from sleep on address match. Each bus line needs one pull-up resistor to the supply. PRTWI in PRR0 must be 0 to use it.

All drivers are open drain or open collector, forming a wired-AND: any device driving 0 pulls a line low, and the pull-ups take it high when all release. Every AVR on the bus must be powered for the bus to work. The number of devices is limited by the 400 pF bus capacitance and the 7-bit address space. Electrical specifications are given separately for bus speeds below 100 kHz and up to 400 kHz.

SDA must be steady while SCL is high, except for START and STOP, which the master signals by changing SDA while SCL is high. The bus is busy from START to STOP. A START issued before a STOP is a repeated START, letting the master begin a new transfer without releasing the bus.

An address packet is 9 bits: 7 address bits MSB first, a read/write bit (1 = read) and an acknowledge bit, in which the addressed slave pulls SDA low; a busy slave leaves it high. These are SLA+R and SLA+W. Address 0000 000 is the general call, to which all enabled slaves acknowledge and then take the following data; general call with a read bit makes no sense. Addresses 1111 xxx are reserved. A data packet is one byte MSB first plus an acknowledge from the receiver; a NACK after the last byte tells the transmitter to stop.

A transmission is a START, then SLA+R/W, then at least one data packet, then a STOP; START followed straight by STOP is illegal. A slave can stretch the SCL low period to slow the master; the high period stays the master's.

Several masters may start at once. Their clocks are wired-ANDed: the bus high time is the shortest master high time and the low time the longest low time, each master counting from the bus edges. Arbitration runs continuously: a master that reads SDA low while sending high has lost, must switch to slave mode at once to see whether it is addressed, and may keep clocking until the end of the packet. Arbitration can run into the data when masters address the same slave. Arbitration is not allowed between a repeated START and a data bit, a STOP and a data bit, or a repeated START and a STOP, so in multi-master systems all transfers must have the same make-up of SLA+R/W and data packets.
The output drivers are slew-rate limited and the inputs remove spikes shorter than 50 ns. The internal pull-ups, set by the PORT bits of SCL and SDA, can replace external ones in some systems.

In master modes TWBR and the prescaler bits in TWSR set the SCL period. Slave operation does not depend on them, but the slave CPU clock must be at least 16 times SCL. Slaves stretching SCL lower the average bus clock.

operation.topic: TWI bus interface and address match
operation.text: The bus interface unit holds TWDR (address or data), the (N)ACK bit (set through TWCR when receiving, read from TWSR when transmitting), START/STOP control and arbitration detection; START and STOP are detected even in sleep. The address match unit compares received addresses with the 7-bit address in TWAR, and with the general call address when TWGCE is set, also in sleep, waking the part. If another interrupt such as INT0 wakes the CPU during a power-down address match, the TWI aborts and goes idle; keeping the address match as the only enabled interrupt in Power-down avoids this.

When a bus event needs the application, TWINT is set and TWSR gets a status code in the next clock; at other times TWSR reads a no-information code. SCL is held low while TWINT is set. TWINT is set after sending START or repeated START, after sending SLA+R/W or an address byte, on losing arbitration, on being addressed by own address or general call, after receiving a data byte, on a STOP or repeated START while still addressed as slave, and on a bus error from an illegal START or STOP.

The TWI is byte oriented and interrupt based, raising an interrupt after every bus event when TWIE and the global interrupt bit are set, otherwise polled through TWINT. At each TWINT the application reads TWSR, loads TWDR with what the next bus cycle needs, then writes TWCR with TWINT set, which clears the flag and starts the next operation; the TWI does nothing while TWINT is set. TWINT is not set after a STOP has been sent. Example, a master writing one byte: START, check status, load SLA+W, check, load data, check, send STOP.

Four modes: Master Transmitter, Master Receiver, Slave Transmitter and Slave Receiver, which an application can mix; for instance MT to write a TWI EEPROM and MR to read it back. Status codes are given with the prescaler bits masked to 0; the transfer waits at each code until TWINT is cleared.

A START is sent once the bus is free, giving status 0x08; writing SLA+W to TWDR and clearing TWINT enters MT mode, after which 0x18, 0x20 or 0x38 can follow. Data bytes are written to TWDR only while TWINT is high, else TWWC is set and the write discarded. The transfer ends with a STOP or a repeated START (status 0x10), which can address the same or another slave, or switch between MT and MR, without releasing the bus.

After START (0x08), writing SLA+R enters MR mode; 0x38, 0x40 or 0x48 can follow. Received bytes are read from TWDR while TWINT is set. After the last byte the master returns NACK, then sends STOP or a repeated START.

TWAR holds the own address in its upper seven bits, with the LSB enabling response to general call; TWCR is written with TWEN and TWEA set. When addressed with a write bit the TWI enters SR mode and sets TWINT; it can also enter on losing arbitration as master (0x68, 0x78). Clearing TWEA makes it return NACK after the next byte and stop acknowledging its address while still watching the bus, which isolates it until TWEA is set again. In sleep modes other than Idle the TWI clock is off, but with TWEA set it can still recognize its address using the bus clock, wake the part and hold SCL low until TWINT is cleared; a long start-up time can thus hold SCL low a long while. After such a wake-up TWDR does not hold the last byte on the bus.

Set up as for Slave Receiver; addressed with a read bit, the TWI enters ST mode, or on lost arbitration (0xB0). Clearing TWEA during a transfer makes the next byte the last: the TWI enters 0xC0 or 0xC8 depending on the master's NACK or ACK, goes to not-addressed slave mode and sends all ones if the master keeps reading. Sleep behaviour is as in Slave Receiver mode.

Status 0xF8 means no information, as TWINT is not set. Status 0x00 is a bus error, a START or STOP in an illegal place such as inside an address, data or acknowledge bit; TWINT is set, and setting TWSTO while clearing TWINT recovers: the TWI enters not-addressed slave mode, clears TWSTO, releases SDA and SCL and sends no STOP.

Reading a serial EEPROM needs MT mode to send the location and MR mode to read it, with the master keeping the bus throughout so that no other master can move the EEPROM's pointer in between: a repeated START separates the address write from the data read.

Masters doing identical transfers to the same slave never notice each other. Masters sending different data or direction to one slave arbitrate in the R/W bit or the data. Masters addressing different slaves arbitrate in the SLA bits; losers switch to slave mode and, if addressed, to SR or ST, else to not-addressed slave mode or wait to send a new START, as software decides.

A USB 2.0 device controller for full speed and low speed, with dual-bank (ping-pong) endpoints held in 832 bytes of dual-port RAM: endpoint 0 of up to 64 bytes as the default control endpoint, one endpoint of up to 256 bytes and five of up to 64 bytes, each with one or two banks. Low speed can run without a crystal.

Full speed needs a 48 MHz clock within ±0.25%, made by the on-chip PLL from the low power crystal oscillator, an external clock or the internal RC oscillator. From it the controller derives the 12 MHz full-speed or 1.5 MHz low-speed bit clock, and a digital PLL recovers the clock from the received data within the USB jitter limits.
The D+ and D- buffers must run from 3.0 V to 3.6 V. Since the part itself may run up to 5.5 V, an internal regulator supplies the USB buffers; its output is the UCAP pin.

In low-speed mode the internal RC oscillator may clock the PLL, saving the crystal; the RC oscillator is factory calibrated to the low-speed frequency accuracy from 0 °C to +40 °C. Full speed needs an external crystal or an external clock.

The series resistors on D+ and D- are 22 Ω ±5%. Tracks from the receptacle (or the cable of a tethered device) to the pins are as short as possible and routed as a differential pair: equal length, close together, few vias. Transient or ESD suppressors may protect the USB pads. The UCAP capacitor is 1 µF ±10%, and a 10 µF capacitor on VBUS is strongly recommended.

Power-on, external, watchdog, brown-out and JTAG resets disable and reset the USB controller. An optional further CPU reset source, the USB end of reset, resets the controller without disabling it, so the device stays attached.

After a hardware reset the controller is in its Reset state: USBE clear, its clock stopped (FRZCLK = 1) to save power, the controller disabled, the pad suspended and the device logic reset. Setting USBE moves it to the Device state, idle. Clearing USBE at any time acts as a hardware reset of the controller.

Two interrupt vectors serve the USB: the general vector, for VBUS transitions (VBUSTI) and the device events upstream resume, end of resume, wake-up, end of reset, start of frame and suspend; and the endpoint vector, for data transfer events. Each endpoint has eight flagged interrupt sources, each with its own enable; UEINT tells which endpoint raised the interrupt. Most events are detected only while the USB clock runs; VBUS plug-in and removal and the WAKEUP event on any change of the data lines are asynchronous and can wake the part from power-down, typically after the bus has gone into suspend.

In Idle the CPU clock stops whether or not the controller runs, and any USB interrupt wakes the CPU. In Power-down every clock stops, and the controller wakes on WAKEUPI or VBUSTI. Setting FRZCLK freezes the controller clock to save power; USBCON, USBSTA, USBINT, UDCON, UDINT and UDIEN stay accessible, and only WAKEUPI and VBUSTI can then trigger.
Speed follows which data line carries the pull-up: LSM in UDCON connects the internal pull-up to D- for low speed or to D+ for full speed, and DETACH disconnects it.

Endpoints must be allocated in increasing number order. Setting an endpoint's ALLOC reserves its memory between the endpoints below and above it; the next endpoint's memory moves up, losing its contents, while higher endpoints stay put. Clearing EPEN keeps ALLOC and the configuration (EPSIZE, EPBK). Clearing ALLOC frees the memory and the next endpoint slides down. Re-allocating an endpoint with a larger size can make two endpoints overlap and lose data, and CFGOK is still set in that case.
