Endpoint 0 data are never lost through other endpoints changing, only when it is deactivated itself; deactivating and reactivating an endpoint with unchanged parameters moves nothing.

The pad runs in an active mode or a low-power idle mode. It is active while USBE = 1, DETACH = 0 and the bus is not suspended. A detected suspend (SUSPI) puts the pad in idle; the next non-idle bus event sets WAKEUPI and wakes it. Setting DETACH also idles the pad until DETACH is cleared.

The VBUS pin's internal session-valid signal is active when VBUS is at or above 1.4 V; it sets the VBUS status bit in USBSTA, and VBUSTI is set on every change. The device cannot attach to the bus while VBUS is not set.

Power on: enable the USB pad regulator, configure and enable the PLL, wait for lock, enable and configure the USB interface (speed, endpoints), wait for VBUS, then attach. Power off: detach, disable the interface, the PLL and the pad regulator. Suspend: clear the suspend flag, freeze the USB clock, disable the PLL, make sure an interrupt can end sleep, then sleep. Resume: enable the PLL, wait for lock, unfreeze the clock and clear the resume flag.

Besides default control endpoint 0 (FIFO up to 64 bytes) there are six endpoints for control, bulk, interrupt or isochronous transfers: endpoint 1 up to 256 bytes and endpoints 2 to 6 up to 64 bytes, all with ping-pong banks. The controller starts in idle, with the pad drawing as little as it can.

After reset the macro clock is stopped (FRZCLK set), all device registers hold their defaults with DETACH set, the endpoint banks are reset and neither data line has its pull-up. The pull-up connects once DETACH is cleared and VBUS is present. The idle state after reset needs no PLL. Clearing USBE resets the device controller at any time.

Setting an endpoint's EPRSTx bit in UERST resets its state machine, clears its banks and their pointers, and returns UEINTX, UESTA0X and UESTA1X to their reset values. The data toggle, the other registers and the endpoint's configuration and enable stay as they were. RSTDT clears the data toggle, as a CLEAR_FEATURE request needs.

An SE0 of at least 2.5 µs on the bus is a USB reset: every endpoint is disabled and the default control endpoint stays configured. With RSTCPU in UDCON set, a USB reset also resets the CPU while the controller stays enabled and attached.

The CPU selects an endpoint by writing its number to EPNUM2:0 in UENUM before touching its registers. An endpoint stays in reset until EPEN is set. Activation: select it, set EPEN, set direction and type in UECFG0X, set size, banks and ALLOC in UECFG1X (memory is allocated at once), then check CFGOK. Until CFGOK is set the hardware does not acknowledge host packets; CFGOK stays clear if the size exceeds the DPRAM. Clearing EPEN resets the endpoint and its data toggle but keeps its configuration and its DPRAM reservation.

The device answers at address 0 after power-up. On SET_ADDRESS the firmware writes the address to UADD with ADDEN still clear, sends a zero-length IN packet, then sets ADDEN; from then on only the UADD address is accepted. ADDEN and UADD are not written together. UADD is 00h after power-up or a USB reset; ADDEN is cleared by power-up reset, a USB reset or clearing USBE, and address 00h is used while it is clear.

After 3 ms of bus inactivity the controller switches to full-speed mode and raises SUSPI if enabled; firmware may then set FRZCLK and put the CPU in idle. To recover, clear FRZCLK if the CPU is running, or with the CPU idle enable WAKEUPE: any non-idle signal raises WAKEUPI, and the firmware then clears FRZCLK. WAKEUPI fires on any non-idle line activity, suspended or not; each of SUSPI and WAKEUPI clears the other when it is set.

DETACH resets to 1. Setting and then clearing it disconnects and reconnects the D+ or D- pull-up (whichever the speed selects), which makes the host enumerate the device again; firmware allows a debounce delay of a few milliseconds.

Upstream resume is the only bus action the device may start itself, and only after the host has sent DEVICE_REMOTE_WAKEUP and the bus is suspended (SUSPI set). Setting RMWKUP sends the resume signal once the bus has been idle 5 ms; UPRSMI is raised as it starts and SUSPI is cleared, RMWKUP clears at its end, and a proper end of resume from the host raises EORSMI.

Setting STALLRQ makes the endpoint answer every following request with STALL until STALLRQC is set; STALLRQC clears STALLRQ and clears itself at once, so it always reads 0. Each STALL sent sets STALLEDI and can raise the endpoint interrupt; incoming packets are dropped without setting RXOUTI or RWAL. When the host clears the stall, firmware sets STALLRQC and resets the endpoint. A SETUP on a control endpoint is always acknowledged, even with a stall requested, and it clears the stall request and flags, which simplifies enumeration. A retry takes priority over a STALL.

A SETUP packet is always acknowledged and sets RXSTPI, not RXOUTI. FIFOCON and RWAL have no meaning on control endpoints and read 0. Firmware clears RXSTPI to acknowledge a SETUP and free the bank, clears RXOUTI likewise for OUT data, and clears TXINI to send an IN packet. In a control write the status stage can be answered early with a zero-length packet, or the firmware can poll NAKINI to learn that the host has moved to the status stage. In a control read the first status-stage token is NAKed; once the status stage is detected, data the CPU wrote is discarded and clearing TXINI does nothing; an OUT retry is always acknowledged and sets both RXOUTI and TXINI. The byte counter resets on the OUT zero-length packet. After the OUT status stage the controller waits for the next SETUP, which takes priority over everything else.

When the current bank fills, RXOUTI and FIFOCON are set, raising the endpoint interrupt if RXOUTE is set. The CPU clears RXOUTI, reads the byte count BYCT, reads that many bytes through UEDATX, then clears FIFOCON to free the bank (or once RWAL goes clear). RXOUTI is always cleared before FIFOCON. With two banks the host can fill one while the CPU reads the other, so RXOUTI may set again at once. RWAL shows whether the current bank still holds data to read.

When the current bank is free, TXINI and FIFOCON are set, raising the interrupt if TXINE is set. The CPU clears TXINI, writes the data through UEDATX, then clears FIFOCON to let the controller send it and move to the next bank. TXINI is always cleared before FIFOCON. RWAL shows whether the current bank can take more data.

The host can abort an IN stage, for instance with a zero-length OUT packet during a control or isochronous IN stage. KILLBK kills the last written bank. Abort sequence: clear TXINE; while NBUSYBK is not 0, set KILLBK and wait for it to clear; then reset the endpoint.

An IN token on an empty bank, or an OUT packet arriving while all banks are full (the packet is lost), is an underflow and sets UNDERFI. A bad CRC on an OUT packet sets STALLEDI and still sets RXOUTI. On any endpoint type, an OUT packet larger than the bank sets OVERFI; the packet is acknowledged, RXOUTI is set, and the bank holds the packet's first bytes. The CPU side cannot under- or overflow if it reads and writes only when RXOUTI, TXINI or RWAL allows.

Normal processing interrupts: VBUSTI when VBUS appears or goes, UPRSMI when upstream resume starts, EORSMI when resume ends, WAKEUPI on line activity, EORSTI when a bus reset ends (speed set), SOFI on each start of frame with FNCERR = 0, and SUSPI after 3 ms idle; the exception is a CRC error in a SOF frame number (SOFI with FNCERR = 1). Per endpoint, processing interrupts are ready for IN data (TXINI), OUT data received (RXOUTI) and SETUP received (RXSTPI); exceptions are stall sent (STALLEDI), isochronous CRC error (STALLEDI), isochronous overflow (OVERFI) and underflow (UNDERFI), NAK IN sent (NAKINI) and NAK OUT sent (NAKOUTI).

Compares AIN+ with AIN- and sets ACO while AIN+ is the higher. Its output can trigger the Timer/Counter1 input capture and has its own interrupt, on a rising edge, falling edge or toggle. AIN+ is the AIN0 pin (PE6) or the internal bandgap reference; AIN- comes through the ADC multiplexer. PRADC in PRR0 must be 0 for the ADC multiplexer to be usable.

With ACIC set the comparator output drives the Timer/Counter1 input capture logic directly, using its noise canceler and edge select; ICIE1 in TIMSK1 enables the capture interrupt. With ACIC clear there is no link.
With ACME set and the ADC off (ADEN = 0), MUX2:0 in ADMUX choose an ADC pin as the comparator's negative input in place of the default. With ACME clear or ADEN set, the bandgap reference is used.

10-bit successive approximation ADC (8-bit option) with 0.5 LSB integral non-linearity and ±2 LSB absolute accuracy; 65 µs to 260 µs conversion time, up to 15 kSPS at full resolution; twelve multiplexed single-ended channels; one differential amplifier with gains of 1x, 10x, 40x and 200x; temperature sensor; optional left-adjusted result; 0 to VCC input range; selectable 2.56 V reference; free running or single conversion, auto triggering from interrupt sources, conversion complete interrupt and sleep mode noise canceler.

The ADC sits behind an analog multiplexer for single-ended inputs on pins of ports B, D and F, referred to GND, and offers 32 differential input combinations through a programmable gain amplifier ahead of conversion. Two differential channels share ADC0/ADC1 as common negative input and any other ADC input may be the positive one. Expect 8-bit resolution at 1x, 10x or 40x gain and 7-bit at 200x. A sample-and-hold keeps the input constant during conversion. AVCC, the separate analog supply, must stay within ±0.3 V of VCC. Internal references of nominally 2.56 V or AVCC are available, and AREF can be decoupled with a capacitor for lower noise.

The 10-bit result runs from GND (minimum) to the AREF voltage less 1 LSB (maximum). AVCC or the internal 2.56 V reference can be switched to AREF with the REFSn bits in ADMUX. The MUX bits pick the input channel and differential gain; any ADC pin, GND or the bandgap can be a single-ended input. ADEN in ADCSRA enables the ADC; reference and channel choices take effect only once it is set, and the ADC draws no power with ADEN clear, so it is best turned off before power-saving sleep. The result sits in ADCH and ADCL, right adjusted unless ADLAR is set. For 8 bits from a left-adjusted result, ADCH alone suffices; otherwise read ADCL first, which blocks updates until ADCH is read, so a conversion finishing in between is lost though its interrupt still fires.

Writing 1 to ADSC starts a single conversion; ADSC stays 1 until it ends. A channel change during a conversion waits until that conversion completes. With ADATE set, a rising edge on the trigger source chosen by ADTS in ADCSRB resets the prescaler and starts a conversion, giving fixed intervals; a trigger still high at the end, or a new edge during conversion, starts nothing. The trigger's interrupt flag is set even with its interrupt disabled, and it must be cleared before the next event can trigger. Using ADIF as the trigger gives free running mode, started by one write to ADSC and continuing whether or not ADIF is cleared. ADSC reads 1 during any conversion, however started.

Full 10-bit resolution needs an ADC clock from 50 kHz to 200 kHz; for lower resolution the clock can be higher for more samples per second. ADHSM in ADCSRB allows a faster ADC clock at the cost of more power. A 7-bit prescaler, set by ADPS in ADCSRA, divides the CPU clock by 2 to 128 and suits any CPU clock above 100 kHz; it counts while ADEN is set and is held reset while ADEN is clear.

A single-ended conversion started by ADSC begins on the next rising ADC clock edge. Normal conversions last 13 ADC clock cycles; the first one after enabling the ADC lasts 25, to initialize the analog circuits. In a normal conversion sample-and-hold falls 1.5 ADC clocks after the start. At the end the result is written and ADIF set, and in single conversion mode ADSC clears at the same time. With auto triggering the prescaler resets on the trigger, so the delay to the start is fixed; sample-and-hold falls two ADC clocks after the trigger edge, and synchronization adds three CPU clocks. In free running mode the next conversion starts as soon as one ends, with ADSC staying high.

Differential conversions are synchronized to CKADC2, half the ADC clock. A conversion the user starts (single conversions and the first free running one) takes 13 ADC clocks if CKADC2 is low and 14 if it is high; the automatically started free running conversions all take 14. With auto triggering, a differential conversion is invalid because the prescaler reset upsets the gain stage, so the ADC is turned off and on between conversions; only extended conversions then run, and their results are valid. The gain stage is optimized for 4 kHz bandwidth at every gain; higher frequencies may be amplified non-linearly, so inputs with higher-frequency content need an external low-pass filter. The ADC clock does not depend on this limit: a 6 µs ADC clock period samples a channel at 12 kSPS whatever its bandwidth.

MUXn and REFS1:0 pass through a buffer register: the selection follows writes until a conversion starts, is then locked, and resumes following in the last ADC clock before completion (ADIF). Since the conversion starts on the ADC clock edge after ADSC is written, new values are written no sooner than one ADC clock after ADSC. With ADATE and ADEN both set an interrupt event can come at any time, so ADMUX is changed safely only with ADATE or ADEN clear, during a conversion at least one ADC clock after the trigger, or after a conversion before the triggering flag is cleared; the new setting then applies to the next conversion. After selecting a new differential channel the gain stage needs up to 125 µs to settle; conversions in that time are not started or are discarded. The same settling applies to the first differential conversion after a reference change. Settling time and gain-stage bandwidth do not depend on ADHSM.

In single conversion mode select the channel before starting; it may change one ADC clock after ADSC is written, but waiting for the conversion to finish is simplest. In free running mode select the channel before the first conversion; changing it after a conversion completes affects the conversion after next, because the next one has already started on the old channel. The first result after switching to a differential gain channel may be poor while the automatic offset cancellation settles and is best discarded.

VREF sets the conversion range; single-ended inputs above it read close to 0x3FF. VREF is AVCC, the internal 2.56 V reference or an external voltage on AREF. AVCC reaches the ADC through a passive switch; the 2.56 V reference is made from the bandgap VBG by an internal amplifier. Either way AREF is connected straight to the ADC, so a capacitor from AREF to ground lowers reference noise, and VREF can be measured there with a high-impedance voltmeter. VREF is a high-impedance source and only a capacitive load belongs on it. With a fixed voltage applied to AREF the internal options must not be selected, since they would be shorted to it; with nothing on AREF the user can switch between AVCC and 2.56 V. The first result after switching reference may be inaccurate and is best discarded. For differential channels the reference must not come closer to AVCC than the limit in the ADC characteristics.

An on-chip temperature sensor drives a single-ended ADC input selected through MUX5:0 in ADMUX, and is read with the internal 2.56 V reference in single conversion mode. Selecting it also turns on its driver, whose propagation delay is about 2 µs, so the first conversion is discarded and the second used; selecting it just after the start of the preceding conversion lets one conversion suffice.

The sensor is linear but its initial tolerance is ±10 °C, so accurate temperature readings need a calibration in firmware. In production a two-point calibration at +25 °C and +85 °C (each ±10 °C) stores the sensor readings Ti in EEPROM and the OSCCAL values Oi giving an accurate 8 MHz at those temperatures in another memory area; with these four values and the linear behaviour of sensor and RC oscillator, firmware can re-trim the RC oscillator as temperature changes. Because the production temperatures are only ±10 °C, these values do not give an accurate thermometer. A chip erase clears the EEPROM calibration values unless the EESAVE fuse is programmed.

The ADC can convert in sleep to escape CPU and I/O noise, in ADC Noise Reduction or Idle mode: with the ADC enabled, idle, in single conversion mode and with its complete interrupt enabled, enter the sleep mode; the conversion starts once the CPU halts. If no other interrupt comes first, the ADC interrupt wakes the CPU; if another wakes it first, that interrupt runs and the ADC interrupt follows when the conversion completes, the CPU staying awake until the next SLEEP. Other sleep modes do not turn the ADC off, so ADEN is cleared before entering them. For differential conversions after waking with the ADC enabled, turn it off and on to force a valid extended conversion.

An ADCn pin always loads its source with its pin capacitance and leakage, selected or not. When selected, the source charges the 14 pF sample-and-hold capacitor through 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ of series resistance. The ADC is optimized for sources of about 10 kΩ or less, for which sampling time is negligible; a higher-impedance source needs longer to charge the capacitor, so low-impedance sources and slow signals are best. For differential gain channels the source impedance should stay at or below a few hundred kΩ. Neither channel type should carry signals above the Nyquist frequency fADC/2; a low-pass filter removes them before the input.

Keep analog paths short, over the analog ground plane and away from fast digital tracks. Feed AVCC from VCC through an LC network (10 µH and 100 nF). Use the ADC noise canceler. ADC port pins used as digital outputs must not switch while a conversion runs.

The gain stage nulls the offset of differential measurements as far as it can. The rest can be measured with one channel chosen as both differential inputs, then subtracted in software, which brings the offset of any channel below one LSB.

An n-bit single-ended ADC maps GND to VREF linearly onto 2^n codes, the lowest read as 0 and the highest as 2^n − 1. Offset: deviation of the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) from its ideal point at 0.5 LSB; ideal 0 LSB. Gain error: after removing offset, deviation of the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) from its ideal point 1.5 LSB below full scale; ideal 0 LSB. Integral non-linearity: after removing offset and gain error, the largest deviation of any transition from ideal; ideal 0 LSB. Differential non-linearity: the largest deviation of a code width from the ideal 1 LSB; ideal 0 LSB. Quantization error: always ±0.5 LSB, since a 1 LSB span of input maps to one code. Absolute accuracy: the largest deviation of any unadjusted transition from ideal, combining all the above; ideal ±0.5 LSB.

With ADMUX = 0xE9 and MUX5 = 0 (ADC1 − ADC0, 10x gain, 2.56 V reference, left adjusted), 300 mV on ADC1 and 500 mV on ADC0 give ADCR = 512 × 10 × (300 − 500) / 2560 = −400 = 0x270: ADCL reads 0x00 and ADCH 0x9C, or with ADLAR = 0 ADCL reads 0x70 and ADCH 0x02.

An IEEE 1149.1 JTAG interface used for board test through boundary scan, for programming Flash, EEPROM, fuses and lock bits, and for on-chip debugging. The debugger reaches all peripherals, internal and external RAM, the register file, the program counter and the EEPROM and Flash, and can break on the AVR BREAK instruction, a change of program flow, a single step, or program or data memory addresses and address ranges. A TAP controller driven by TCK and TMS selects the instruction register or one of the data registers (ID, bypass, boundary-scan chain, programming interface, and the internal and break point scan chains used only for debugging) as the path from TDI to TDO. The on-chip debug instructions are private, given only to Atmel and selected third parties.

Four pins form the TAP: TMS (state machine control), TCK (clock), TDI (serial data in to the instruction or data register) and TDO (serial data out). The optional TRST is not provided. With the JTAGEN fuse unprogrammed the four pins are ordinary port pins (PF4 to PF7) and the TAP controller is held in reset; programmed, the TAP inputs are pulled up internally and JTAG is available for boundary scan and programming. Parts ship with JTAGEN programmed. For debugging, the debugger also watches R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ to see external resets, and can pull it low to reset the system if only open-collector drivers share the reset line.

A 16-state machine steps on each rising TCK edge according to TMS and starts in Test-Logic-Reset after power-on reset. Shift registers move LSB first. From Run-Test/Idle, TMS = 1, 1, 0, 0 reaches Shift-IR, where the 4-bit instruction shifts in from TDI with TMS low for the three LSBs and high for the MSB, which leaves the state; meanwhile the captured value 0x01 shifts out on TDO. TMS = 1, 1, 0 returns to Run-Test/Idle, the instruction latching in Update-IR. TMS = 1, 0, 0 reaches Shift-DR, where the selected data register shifts in the same way, MSB with TMS high, while the value captured in Capture-DR shifts out; TMS = 1, 1, 0 returns to Run-Test/Idle, latching in Update-DR. Run-Test/Idle need not be visited between instruction and data, and some instructions act in it. Holding TMS high for five TCK periods always reaches Test-Logic-Reset.

Debug hardware: a scan chain between the CPU and the peripherals, a break point unit, and a communication interface between CPU and JTAG. The debugger works by feeding AVR instructions through the CPU scan chain, with results passed back through an I/O-mapped location. The break point unit gives breaks on a program-flow change or after a single step, a pair of program memory break points and a pair of combined ones, usable as four program memory break points; three program and one data; two program and two data; two program and one masked program range; or two program and one masked data range. A debugger may reserve some of these. Debugging needs JTAGEN and OCDEN programmed and no lock bits set; programming LB1 or LB2 disables the debug system so that it cannot open a secured part.

With a debugger the user can run, single step (into or over functions), step out, run to the cursor, stop and reset the target, with any number of code break points placed as BREAK instructions plus at most two data break points, or one masked range.

OCDR is a channel from the running program to the debugger: writing it passes a byte and sets the IDRD (I/O debug register dirty) flag, which the CPU reads as the MSB while the lower seven bits come from OCDR; the debugger clears IDRD after reading. Where OCDR shares an I/O location, it is reached only with OCDEN programmed and the debugger enabling it; otherwise the ordinary I/O location is accessed.

Only TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO plus power are needed, with no 12 V. It needs JTAGEN programmed and JTD in MCUCR at 0. Flash, EEPROM, fuses and lock bits can be programmed and verified. Lock bit security is as in parallel programming: with LB1 or LB2 programmed, OCDEN cannot be programmed until a chip erase, so a secured part cannot be read out.

The boundary-scan chain drives and observes the digital I/O pins and the digital side of analog circuits with off-chip connections, so boards can be tested through the four TAP signals with all JTAG devices chained TDI to TDO. The mandatory IDCODE, BYPASS, SAMPLE/PRELOAD and EXTEST instructions and the public AVR_RESET serve board test; IDCODE is the default, so the first scan shows the device ID. Holding the part in reset during test is advisable so that scanned inputs cannot leave the software in an unknown state; in reset every port output is high impedance, which makes HIGHZ unnecessary. Reset comes from R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ low or AVR_RESET. EXTEST drives the chain's output latches onto the pins as soon as it is loaded, so SAMPLE/PRELOAD first sets safe values; SAMPLE/PRELOAD also takes a snapshot of the pins in normal running. JTAGEN programmed and JTD clear enable the TAP. TCK may run faster than the chip clock, and the chip clock need not run.

The bypass register is one stage, reset to 0 on leaving Capture-DR, and shortens the chain while other devices are tested. The 32-bit device identification register holds version, part number and manufacturer ID. The reset register is a one-bit test register: a 1 acts like R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ held low, and after it returns to 0 the part stays in reset for the reset time-out set by the clock fuses; its output is not latched, so reset is immediate. The boundary-scan chain covers the port pins.

operation.topic: JTAG disable bit and JTAG reset flag
operation.text: JTD in MCUCR disables the JTAG interface when 1; with JTD 0 the interface works if JTAGEN is programmed. To change JTD, software writes the new value twice within four cycles; JTD must not change while the on-chip debug system is in use. JTRF in MCUSR is set by a reset from the JTAG reset register (AVR_RESET) and cleared by power-on reset or by writing 0.

Each bidirectional port pin's cell folds output control (OC), output data (OD) and input data (ID) into a two-stage shift register; pull-ups are disabled while the instruction register holds EXTEST or SAMPLE_PRELOAD. With no alternate function active, ID is the pin value as PINxn shows it but without the synchronizer, OD is the PORT bit and OC the DDR bit. Digital alternate functions connect outside the scanned cell so the chain reads the real pin value; analog functions connect straight to the pin. During EXTEST or SAMPLE_PRELOAD the clock output selected by CKOUT is not sampled by the chain.
R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ takes 5 V active-low logic for normal reset and a 12 V high level that enters high-voltage parallel programming. The 5 V reset signal has an observe-only cell in the chain.

Bit 0 is the LSB, first in and first out. The order follows the pinout as far as it can, with analog circuit chains taking the most significant bits wherever their pins are. PF4 to PF7 are left out because they are the TAP pins when JTAG is enabled, and the USB pads are not scanned.
Boundary-scan description language (BSDL) files describing the chain, the order and function of its bits, exist for the device for use by automatic test generation software.

A Flash-resident boot loader can download and upload program code through any interface the MCU has, while the rest of the program keeps running (read-while-write). Code in the boot loader section can write the whole Flash, the boot loader included, so it can update or erase itself. Its size is set by fuses, and two separate sets of boot lock bits give independent protection. It offers a choice of boot sizes, independent boot lock bits, a fuse choosing the reset vector, an optimized page size, compact code and read-modify-write support.

The Flash splits into an application section and a boot loader section (BLS), sized by the BOOTSZ fuses and protected by separate lock bits: boot lock bits 0 for the application section and boot lock bits 1 for the BLS. SPM can start programming only when executed from the BLS, so boot loader code must sit there and the application section can never hold it. SPM from the BLS reaches the whole Flash.

Independently of the BOOTSZ split, the Flash has two fixed sections, RWW and NRWW. While a page in the RWW section is erased or written, code in the NRWW section can still be read and run; while a page in the NRWW section is erased or written, the CPU is halted throughout. The name refers to the section being programmed, not the one being read. Code in the RWW section can never be read during a boot loader operation: reading it then (through a load, call, jump or interrupt) can leave software in an unknown state, so interrupts are disabled or moved to the BLS, which always lies in the NRWW section. RWWSB in SPMCSR reads 1 while the RWW section is blocked, and software clears it after programming before reading code there.

Without a boot loader the whole Flash is available to the application. The boot lock bits can protect the whole Flash from software update, only the BLS, only the application section, or nothing. Software, serial programming and parallel programming can all set them; only chip erase clears them. Lock bit mode 2 (general write lock) does not restrict SPM, and lock bit mode 1 (general read/write lock) does not restrict (E)LPM or SPM.

The boot loader runs after a jump or call from the application (for instance on a command received over USART, SPI or USB); after reset when the BOOTRST fuse is programmed, which points the reset vector at the boot loader start; or, with the HWBE fuse programmed, when the ALE/HWB pin is low at the rising edge of reset. The MCU cannot alter its own fuses, so BOOTRST once programmed is changed only through serial or parallel programming. With HWBE programmed, ALE/HWB is an input during reset and is sampled on the reset rising edge, with setup tSHRH and hold tHHRH.

SPMCSR holds the boot loader control bits. SPMIE with the global interrupt bit enables the SPM ready interrupt, which runs while SPMEN is clear. RWWSB is set by hardware when a page erase or write to the RWW section starts and blocks that section; it clears when RWWSRE is written after the operation, or when a page load starts. SIGRD written with SPMEN makes an LPM within three clock cycles read the signature row.

SPM commands are addressed by the Z-pointer (ZH:ZL). Its low bits select a word within a page and its high bits select this page. Page erase and page write are addressed separately, so both must name the same page. Once an operation starts the address is latched and Z is free for other use. (E)LPM addresses Flash by byte and so also uses Z0.

Flash is updated a page at a time, erasing a page before writing it from the temporary page buffer. Words go into the buffer singly, either before the erase or between erase and write. Filling it first allows read-modify-write: read a page, change it in the buffer, erase, write. Filling after the erase cannot recover the old data. Words not being changed must be saved, for instance in the buffer, before the erase. The buffer can be written in any order. The temporary buffer clears itself after a page write, when RWWSRE is written or on reset, and each address can be written only once between clears. An EEPROM write during page loading loses all the loaded data.

operation.topic: SPM interrupt and protecting the boot loader
operation.text: With the SPM interrupt enabled, an interrupt is raised continuously while SPMEN is clear, so it can replace polling; the interrupt vectors should then be in the BLS so that no interrupt reaches the blocked RWW section. If the BLS is left writable (boot lock bit 11 unprogrammed), a stray write can corrupt the boot loader and stop all later updates, so programming boot lock bit 11 is recommended when the boot loader never needs changing. During self-programming the RWW section stays blocked: software keeps away from it, moves the vectors to the BLS or disables interrupts, and writes RWWSRE afterwards before using it.

operation.topic: Setting boot lock bits by SPM
operation.text: Write the wanted value to R0 (bits 5 to 2 are BLB12, BLB11, BLB02, BLB01; bits 7, 6, 1 and 0 set to 1), load SPMCSR with X0001001 and follow with SPM inside four cycles; a cleared bit programs its lock bit. Only the boot lock bits can be set this way. Z is don't care, though 0x0001 is recommended. The whole Flash stays readable during the operation.
An EEPROM write blocks all software programming of the Flash, and blocks software reads of fuses and lock bits; checking that EEPE in EECR is clear before writing SPMCSR is recommended.

operation.topic: Reading fuses, lock bits and signature from software
operation.text: Load Z with the byte's address, set BLBSET and SPMEN in SPMCSR, and execute (E)LPM within three CPU cycles: the lock bits, fuse low, high or extended byte lands in the destination register. BLBSET and SPMEN clear when the read completes, or if no (E)LPM follows within three cycles or no SPM within four. The signature row is read the same way with SIGRD and SPMEN set and LPM within three cycles.

At low VCC the Flash can be corrupted, both because a write needs a minimum voltage and because the CPU may execute instructions wrongly. Any one of these avoids it: program the boot lock bits if the boot loader never needs updating; hold R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ active while the supply is too low, using the internal brown-out detector if its level fits or an external reset circuit, noting that a write in progress completes if the supply allows; or keep the core in power-down sleep while VCC is low, so it cannot decode instructions that would write SPMCSR.
Six lock bits, unprogrammed (1) or programmed (0), add the protections listed in the lock bit tables; they return to 1 only through chip erase.

Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode, so changes take effect only after leaving it, except EESAVE, which acts as soon as it is programmed. Fuses are also latched at power-up in normal mode.
The internal RC oscillator's calibration value sits in the signature address space as the upper byte at address 0x000 and is copied into OSCCAL during reset.

Flash, EEPROM, lock bits and fuses can be programmed and verified in parallel mode. Pulses are at least 250 ns long unless stated otherwise. XA1 and XA0 choose what a positive pulse on XTAL1 does, BS2 and BS1 choose the byte, and the loaded command decides what a pulse on W̅R̅ or O̅E̅ does.

Apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V between VCC and GND. Hold R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ at 0 and toggle XTAL1 at least six times. Set PAGEL, XA1, XA0 and BS1 to 0000 and wait at least 100 ns. Apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅; any change on those four pins within 100 ns after this makes entry fail. Wait at least 50 µs before the next command.

Command and address are retained, so a command is loaded once for many locations; 0xFF data need not be written after a chip erase (in EEPROM only if EESAVE is unprogrammed); and the address high byte is loaded only when moving to a new 256-word Flash or 256-byte EEPROM window, which also applies to reading signature bytes.

Chip erase clears Flash, EEPROM (kept if EESAVE is programmed) and lock bits, the lock bits only after the Flash is fully erased; fuses are unchanged. It must precede reprogramming Flash or EEPROM. Load command 1000 0000 (XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, pulse XTAL1), give W̅R̅ a negative pulse, and wait for RDY/B̅S̅Y̅ to go high.

Flash data go through a page buffer, a page at a time. A: load command 0001 0000. B: load the address low byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS2:BS1 = 00). C: load the data low byte (XA1:XA0 = 01). D: load the data high byte (BS1 = 1, XA1:XA0 = 01). E: latch the data with a positive PAGEL pulse (BS1 = 1). F: repeat B to E until its page buffer is full. G: load the address high byte (BS2:BS1 = 01). H: load the address extended high byte (BS2:BS1 = 10). I: with BS2:BS1 = 00 give W̅R̅ a negative pulse to program this page and wait for RDY/B̅S̅Y̅ to go high. J: repeat B to I for every page. K: end by loading command 0000 0000 (no operation), which resets the internal write signals. The low address bits pick the word in this page and the higher bits this page; with pages under 256 words the top bits of the address low byte address this page.

Through a page buffer, a page at a time: load command 0001 0001, the address high byte, then for each byte the address low byte, the data and a PAGEL latch pulse; with BS2:BS1 = 00 a negative W̅R̅ pulse programs this page, and RDY/B̅S̅Y̅ going high marks the end.

operation.topic: Parallel reading of Flash and EEPROM
operation.text: Flash: load command 0000 0010, the extended, high and low address bytes, then with O̅E̅ = 0 and BS1 = 0 the word's low byte appears on DATA, and with BS1 = 1 its high byte; finish with O̅E̅ = 1. EEPROM: load command 0000 0011, the high and low address bytes, then O̅E̅ = 0 and BS1 = 0 gives the byte.

operation.topic: Parallel fuse and lock bit programming
operation.text: Load command 0100 0000 and the new value as a data low byte (0 programs a bit, 1 erases it), select the byte with BS2:BS1 (00 low, 01 high, 10 extended), give W̅R̅ a negative pulse and wait for RDY/B̅S̅Y̅, then return BS2:BS1 to 00. Lock bits: command 0010 0000, a data low byte with 0 for each bit to program, a W̅R̅ pulse. With LB mode 3 programmed the boot lock bits cannot be programmed by any external programming mode, and lock bits clear only by chip erase.

operation.topic: Parallel reading of fuses, lock bits, signature and calibration
operation.text: Load command 0000 0100, set O̅E̅ = 0 and read DATA with BS2:BS1 = 00 for the fuse low byte, 11 for the fuse high byte, 10 for the extended fuse byte and 01 for the lock bits (0 = programmed). Signature: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00 to 0x02, O̅E̅ = 0 and BS1 = 0. Calibration byte: command 0000 1000, address 0x00, O̅E̅ = 0 and BS1 = 1.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over a serial bus of SCK, PDI (input) and PDO (output) while R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ is held at GND; the Programming Enable instruction comes first. In serial mode only, EEPROM writes include an automatic erase, so no chip erase is needed first; chip erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. Data into the part are clocked on the rising SCK edge and data out on the falling edge.

Apply power with R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ and SCK at 0; if SCK cannot be guaranteed low during power-up, pulse R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ positive for at least two CPU clocks after SCK is 0. Wait at least 20 ms, then send Programming Enable on PDI. In sync, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third is sent; all four bytes are sent regardless, and without the echo R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ is pulsed and the command repeated. Flash is loaded a byte at a time with Load Program Memory Page (low byte before high byte for each address) and stored with Write Program Memory Page, after Load Extended Address Byte has set the address MSB; that byte is kept until reissued, so it is needed for the first page and when crossing a 64K-word boundary. Without polling RDY/B̅S̅Y̅, wait tWD_FLASH per page; accessing the interface before a write finishes can corrupt it. EEPROM is written a byte at a time, each erased automatically, waiting tWD_EEPROM without polling; 0xFF need not be written to an erased part. Reads verify any location, Flash reads also using the extended address byte. Finish by taking R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ high; to power off, set R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ to 1 and then turn VCC off.

JTAG programming uses only TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO; reset and clock pins need no control. JTAGEN must be programmed (it is at shipment) and JTD in MCUCR clear; alternatively, with JTD set, forcing external reset low clears JTD after two chip clocks and frees the JTAG pins for programming, so they can be port pins in normal running and still serve in-system programming. This does not work for boundary scan or on-chip debug, which need the pins dedicated. TCK must stay below the chip's maximum frequency, and the system clock prescaler cannot divide TCK down. Shift registers move LSB first. Run-Test/Idle generates internal clocks and also serves as idle state between sequences.

operation.topic: JTAG page load and page read
operation.text: PROG_PAGELOAD alternates low and high bytes on each Update-DR, starting with the low byte, and pre-increments the program counter before each low byte except the first, so loading starts at the address set by PROG_COMMANDS and the last word does not step into the next page. PROG_PAGEREAD alternates on each Capture-DR, starting with the low byte, and post-increments after each high byte including the first, so reading starts at the set address and reading the last location steps into the next page.

The reset register (a 1 holds the part as if external reset were low, with the reset time-out after release, not latched) must be set before entering programming mode. The 16-bit programming enable register enables JTAG programming when it holds the signature 0b1010_0011_0111_0000 (0xA370); it clears on power-on reset and should be cleared on leaving programming mode. The 15-bit programming command register shifts commands in and the previous command's result out.

An 8-bit scan chain and an 8-bit temporary register load a whole page buffer before page write, or read out the Flash, shifting only data. During page load Update-DR copies the chain to the temporary register and starts a write into the Flash page buffer that completes within 11 TCK cycles; during page read Capture-DR loads the selected byte. Shifting eight bits per byte gives the state machine enough TCK cycles on its own; if fewer bits are shifted, staying in Run-Test/Idle keeps at least 11 TCK cycles between Update-DR states.

Enter: AVR_RESET with 1 in the reset register, then PROG_ENABLE with 0b1010_0011_0111_0000. Leave: PROG_COMMANDS, no-operation 11a, PROG_ENABLE with all zeros, AVR_RESET with 0. Chip erase: PROG_COMMANDS, 1a, then poll with 1b or wait tWLRH_CE. A chip erase precedes Flash or EEPROM programming. Flash: PROG_COMMANDS, 2a, address bytes 2b to 2d, data 2e to 2g for each word, page write 2h, then poll 2i or wait tWLRH. Faster: after 2a and a page address (PCWORD = 0), PROG_PAGELOAD shifts the whole page byte by byte from the LSB of the first word to the MSB of the last, then PROG_COMMANDS and 2h. Reading Flash: 3a, address 3b to 3d, data 3e, or PROG_PAGEREAD for a whole page, whose first byte out is already valid because Capture-DR precedes Shift-DR. EEPROM: 4a to 4g, and 5a to 5d to read; page load and page read instructions do not work on EEPROM. Fuses: 6a to 6j with a poll or tWLRH after each byte. Lock bits: 7a to 7d. Fuses and lock bits are read with 8a and the 8 instructions, the signature with 9a to 9c at addresses 0x00 to 0x02, and the calibration byte with 10a to 10c at address 0x00.

Driving XTAL1 from an external clock: the high time tCHCX and low time tCLCX are measured at the VIH1 and VIL1 levels, the rise time tCLCH and fall time tCHCL between them, and tCLCL is one full period.
The highest allowed clock frequency rises in a straight line from 8 MHz at VCC = 2.7 V to 16 MHz at 4.5 V and stays at 16 MHz up to 5.5 V.
The 2-wire figures are the requirements on any device connected to the bus; the TWI of this part meets or exceeds them in the conditions given.
For hardware boot entry, ALE/HWB is low at least tSHRH before R̅E̅S̅E̅T̅ goes high and stays low for at least tHHRH after, the start-up time plus time-out delay.

The typical graphs are not tested in production. Current was measured with every I/O pin an input with its pull-up on and a rail-to-rail sine generator as the clock. Active and idle current was taken with all PRR bits set, so the modules are off, and the analog comparator disabled. Power-down current does not depend on the clock chosen. Supply current depends on voltage and frequency above all, and also on I/O loading and switching, the code running and temperature. Parts were characterized above their test limits but are guaranteed only up to the frequency of their ordering code. The watchdog's own current is the difference between power-down current with and without it.
